comments.name: Barbara
comments.body:
I quit my job to take care of my father 30-years ago after he collapsed and was hospitalized for complications from congestive heart failure. My brother's only interest in my father was his inheritance and he was completely out of the picture while my mother had died 15-years earlier so my father was alone. I loved my father very much and promised him that he would never go to a nursing home. 

I don't regret my choice because I loved my father deeply and he was a wonderful man with a positive attitude and a great sense of humor. Our relationship deepened during this time and the memories of our conversations are still with me.

However, it was very hard for me to get back into the work force after his death and I lost years of salary, IRA investments, and social security payments. It's the latter that our government could do something about, but chooses not to and never will. There is no recognition that this service is labor, just as there is no recognition for the labor of stay-at-home mothers.

comments.name: Susan
comments.body: I was Sister-in-Law.  My husband was diagnosed with Parkinson's at 57 and died from its complications when he was 71.  As his wife I willingly took on caregiving responsibilities.  It was very difficult.  It broke my heart.  I was left exhausted, grief-stricken, almost destroyed byt the time he died.  I didn't expect help from his one remaining brother, who lived far away and was still employed.  But the brother, who loved my husband very much, constantly made excuses for not visiting.  I told him to please come before it was too late for my husband to communicate with him.  Well, he arrived too late.  His brother was 3 weeks away from death, though I didn't know that.  He was delirious.  He was in a nursing home for 3 days but was so miserable and the care was so poor that I brought him home.  When Brother arrived he panicked--"You can't take care of him!"  But I did take care of him, not very well sometimes, but I hung in there.  So I had to handle Brother's emotions while my husband made his final trip to the hospital. Brother left, Husband died, and I somehow did all that you have to do when your loved one dies.  Brother was too emotionally fragile to come to the memorial upon which I expended the last of my energy.  I wanted to honor the extraordinary man my husband had been. I know that Brother was truly traumatized and I felt for him.  But Wife's trauma was just part of her duty, not to be taken into any kind of consideration.

comments.name: Tom
comments.body:
There really needs to be a more comprehensive effort across the entire industry, as well as government, to make these things seamless into the digital infrastructure.

Take password managers.  I've been using one for 15 years and recommend doing so to anyone if the subject comes up (though few people listen).  Not just for security but the fact that it relieves the cognitive load of dealing with a zillion passwords. But there are issues. 95+% of the time my password manager (BitWarden, for the record) works perfectly, but some sites do not design their logins with password managers in mind, and in those cases it can be incredibly frustrating even for a tech savvy person.  They also don't integrate easily with anything not in the browser, i.e., standalone programs like Teams or Zoom, which is another headache.  These are the things that keep password managers from widespread adoption.

Over a decade ago, there was the initiatives of Let's Encrypt and HTTPS Everywhere in response to uneven adoption of encryption across the internet.  It worked,..nothing uses unencrypted http anymore.  A broader effort towards seamless easy-to-use integrated security is both possible and necessary, with the onus being on the industry and government to mandate secure design and not leave it to individual users to manage a difficult and frustrating landscape.

comments.name: Arrowroot, son of Arrowshirt
comments.body:
In the several decades of my engineering and manufacturing career, I have seen that management's reluctance to spend money is the major problem followed by their desire to do things quickly. I have not seen evidence of “planned obsolescence,”  as that requires “planning.” 
I have heard too often from marketing that we need to “get it out the door” so we can “meet the market window.” 

Once in a trans-Atlantic phone conversation (before cell phones) involving a couple dozen people - managers, VPs, and lowly engineers - a turbidity probe being designed  by our company was asked about by a British salesman. Our engineer said we were “waiting for the Australian manufacturer to send us two prototypes for testing. The salesman cried, “But I just sold forty!” To which I replied, “That was stupid.”  I was told to shut up or leave the meeting and the engineer was told to have 40 probes drop-shipped to the salesman. Of course they didn’t work and the engineer was blamed.

Too often with complicated products, the people designing one part of a system didn’t talk enough to those working on other parts that needed to work together. It amazes me that failures don’t occur more often.  Designs change more quickly now, so the next version is very different from the previous one and we don’t see the problems arise as much.

comments.name: GFM
comments.body: Baby boomer here.  The solution is simple but now impossible; Eliminate travel sports for youth, and go back to the youth sports model from the 50's thru 80's.  In those days, there were no "travel" sports,  The city recreational departments ran local team programs for football, baseball, and basketball, and teams competed locally in the city or town only.  There were age group programs parallel to junior high and high school teams.  If a kid wanted to play, there was a team somewhere he/she could make.  Team sports teach children lessons they can only learn on the field of competition, teamwork, belonging, spirit, physical and metal toughness, and compassion when your teammate blows the game.  The more serious kids went to "camps" to elevate their skills, but that was the extent of the crazy expenditures.  The model today is very, very, very broken and wasteful of the most precious commodity, childhood.

comments.name: JLW
comments.body:
The sad irony of this piece is that the training model described here is based exactly on the Japanese model of training. Clearly Americans have now realized that they've long been underestimating Japanese talent, which continues to produce MLB stars.

But there's a huge difference. The Japanese system, unlike the hellscape described here, is based on group bonding, not competition. For his entire career with the Nippon Ham Fighters, Shohei Ohtani lived in the team dorm with his teammates, with expenses less than $5K per month. That is why he behaves like a teammate now.

Also built into the Japanese system is the concept of Omenatashi. No task too menial or too difficult to be of service to others. Unrehearsed kindness. The sight of Japanese fans cleaning up the stands at soccer games is now a famous display of Omenatashi. Players in Japanese youth leagues (and their semi-pro women's leagues) practice this too:  grooming practice fields, collecting stray balls, and hauling their own equipment bags. Japanese youth baseball instills humility from  an early age.

Americans have taken their beautiful system and applied our worst instincts: Greed, malice to all, and kindness to none.

I understand the appreciation of the art of the game, the video game. But I have to say, playing Grand Theft Auto rather than reading something that positively feeds your mind and your soul, is a spiritually bankrupting process. Sure, maybe the authors of the game included love and relationships to tamp down criticism of the game’s predatory violence. But that doesn’t mean that grand theft auto is something you should encourage your kids to play. That’s because it’s feeding their limited capacity with images and thoughts. of how to objectify other people. We have enough of that in the world.
How about a good book instead? Or some public television? Or volunteering your time to help someone else? There are lots of alternatives.
If I sound like I’m an old person, it’s because I am, but with age comes experience and wisdom and seeing the hurtful effects of errors human beings live with tomorrow in the choices they make today.

The rank choice system of Alaska is the same as used in Australian (except Tasmanian state elections), and was first called the "Australian system" when first introduced in the early 1920s.
It is a much fairer system than "First Past The Post" used in the U.K. and most U.S. states, as it allows the candidate with the most second preferences to win (on top of their primary vote).

Example, the the recent U.K. by-election in which Mr Farage won, Count Binface got just under 20% if the primary vote. Under a preferential system he would have got over 40%, and if such a system was in place in the U.K. he would have won as more voters would have given him their second preference.

I worry seeing the comments here and in other AI-related posts. I understand people's skepticism of the technology and the motivations of its creators—when have the ultra-wealthy ever looked out for us? I do not blame people for their concerns, but there is a degree of willful ignorance (and minor Luddism) in some of these comments that is striking.

This cat is out of the bag. Don't get me wrong, investments in AI infrastructure may cool off for a year, maybe more. The valuations of equities linked to AI may drop. But anyone who has: a) used frontier models in work; and b) speaks to people who leverage those frontier models at higher levels than themselves, can see that this technology cannot effectively be paused. The benefits derived from using AI for specific applications—robotics training, financial modeling, anything tangentially related to coding—are so immense that you functionally cannot incentivize a global pause. This does not account for the incentives that the wealthy have to continue AI development—to entrench themselves in domains that allow for durable rent-seeking as intelligence becomes less costly. Nor does it account for the incentives of the world's two main sovereigns, the US and China.

We must come to terms with what is ahead and push to restructure society to allow everyone to benefit. Continuing to stick our heads in the sand and argue over whether "we should" is pointless. We ARE. And selfishly, as an American, I prefer our country holds the cards.

Don't let billionaires backing the Heritage Foundation privatize (steal) the FAA systems. If they do the recurring cost (blackmail) will be a crime on the taxpayer.

Say no to Project 2025.

comments.name: Rebecca C.
comments.body: Love this photo illustration.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body: So the author's solution is to create an Air Traffic Control System that works on entirely different principles than the existing system---buy and install all the parts, debug the proramming, traing all the air traffic controllers, and all the pilots on this entirely new structure for air traffic while still launching and landing 20,000 flights a day....

comments.name: PAH
comments.body:
The system is inherently complex and, adding in weather, frequently chaotic.  Current procedures have been built on the blood of pilots (and passengers).  The saying is, if the controller screws up, the pilot dies:  if the pilot screws up, the pilot dies.

Few organizations have the knowledge and resources to build an unhackable new system from scratch, not to mention working out how to handle the transition.  It's not going to come from an organization chosen by friends and family.

comments.name: Sherry
comments.body: I wouldn't trust Duffy with a dime..they dont know what they are doing.

comments.name: Alan
comments.body: I don't know... What would China do???

articles.title: $50 Billion Won’t Fix Air Traffic Control. It Needs to Be Scrapped.
articles.summary: The transportation secretary wants to pour more dollars into an obsolete structure, much like upgrading a Model T for a highway.

comments.name: Smith
comments.body:
Spot on. Mr. Newport articulates so much of what is wrong / bizzare about this company. 

Amodei is talking out of both sides of his mouth. If you want to preserve your control of this technology and truly don't care about making a quick buck, why IPO? And, in the alternative, if you want this technology's development to be shepherded by a diverse, responsible stakeholder base and are truly disinterested in control, why have you structured your company such that you and your sister (with a marketing background) have irrevocable and disproportionate influence? If you truly believe you're building a super weapon and not a fancy search engine, why not cede some of this technology to the government and spearhead a Manhattan-project effort rather than continue to run a publicly-held company?

It feels like Amodei is trying to create the illusion of responsible stewardship when he's in fact doing the opposite.

comments.name: Daniel MacDonald
comments.body: While I agree with the point that going public - even with safeguards such as “Public Benefit Org structure” and board seat/control security hedging tactics - is an immense risk to being able to stay committed to a priority beyond wealth maximization (for fiduciary responsibility-clamoring shareholders), in the absence of agreed upon and concerted INTERNATIONAL efforts to “keep AI safe”, at least one of the main players - and thankfully a powerful leading one - is trying to address the issue by playing their hand seemingly as well as they can.

comments.name: MJ
comments.body:
Anthropic has had all the capital it needed to grow, loaned in vast sums by private investors (many of which are other tech companies) and sovereign funds. It also has had all the control it needed as a private company to try to "save humanity".

The reason it is going public is to offload the risk for all that debt onto the American public.

comments.name: Ellen
comments.body: I'm planning to buy a small position so in the unlikely event of Claude becoming conscious and deciding to destroy humanity I can log into my brokerage and plead for my life with "But I'm a shareholder!!!!"

comments.name: JWC
comments.body:
So much that is so wrong in this op ed! 
Yes, AI may destroy us all. It is certainly changing the world. I do not have to learn to design a website or Keynote presentation. AI can do that for me. It can also compose and perform a pretty good pop song, insert us into a scene from Ancient Rome, or help with interior design choices, build a grocery list, and plan a vacation. 
The boulder is rolling down the hill. We are all playing AI's game. But we have a government that is licking the boots of big tech, and it refused to regulate it or Starlink or SpaceX or pretty much anything that can help lead to that end-times scenario. So, at least Anthropic, unlike every other AI company, has a soul. They will welcome guardrails, it appears. The others will have their technology running AI deadly drones and AI determining missile launches that can kill thousands.

comments.name: Ayn Rant
comments.body:
Before you bet your widows' mite on Silicon Valley's all-knowing, all encompassing Super AI bubble, ponder this! Does the potential profit from subscription fees and advertising revenue from proprietary Super AI models justify the cost of developing and maintaining the software, and building and operating the massive data centers to train and support the models? Guess not! 

There is a better way to manage AI. China continually maintains and improves open-source, limited AI models for  adaptation  to specific social and commercial processes. The adaptations are trained and supported with limited, pertinent data bases. China relegates hazardous Super AI research to "sandboxes" in university labs.

American tech moguls view Super AI as a potential lord and savior of the universe, whereas China views AI as a tool to improve human productivity in building and managing advanced social and physical infrastructures. See the difference?

comments.name: The Sun is eclipsed
comments.body: We have all joked over the years about the fictitious “internet police.”  Perhaps now that’s not such a bad idea?

comments.name: mr
comments.body: I applaud this article. Mr. Newport writes "I don’t fault Mr. Amodei and his company for attempting this experiment in mixing capitalism with ideology" but capitalism mixed with ideology is just capitalism with window dressing. Anthropic are capitalists in the worst way. That's the whole deal.

articles.title: Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game
articles.summary: Trying to save the world and trying to make a lot of money will be an unstable combination.

comments.name: C Franco
comments.body: These 3 did absolutely nothing for their constituents but they leaving with benefits and a pension perhaps? I rather have an illegal, at least they provide something useful

comments.name: Libris Alles
comments.body: I do wonder what comes next for these three. Would you hire them knowing they are not team players if the team is not self aggrandizement? They have shown that they will lie and cheat and steal to enrich themselves. Will their next jobs come from the MAGA uber rich as rewards for their "loyalty" or will they have to go out into the world and see what it's like for "the little people?" Personally, I'd watch where they land and not support any business that thinks they would be an asset. This would tell meu all I need to know about whether that business cares about it's customers and whether it has any moral vertabrae in it's non existant spine.

comments.name: David
comments.body: These people and their superficial ilk hopped onto a bad wagon that was so fashionable several years ago. I can only hope that we get some serious people in Congress who are more interested in serving their constituents rather than making headlines and garnering followers on social media.

comments.name: GEO
comments.body: Well if Steve thinks your too hot what else needs to be said.  They knew their WWE style performative politics would not last.  Especially if there are no good policy results to follow.  MGT's downfall came when she decided to go after Jasmine Crockett.  Crockett's comeback had what I would call a Kendrick Lamar vs Drake affect.  She shrunk after that politically.  At least she was smart enough to exit while still on top,  whatever top was in MAGA.

comments.name: Nina
comments.body: Excellent reporting. May little girls in Texas look up to the decorum and circumspection of Gina Hinojosa now, as we move on. Nina

comments.name: Northpamet
comments.body:
They should start their own political party. 
 Seriously, that is the logical way forward for them.  It will be a good home for that political voice.

comments.name: Yossarian
comments.body: This, and today's article NYT detailing the country's wholesale (at least for now) leftward swing are cause for celebration. Despite the few diehards still manning the MAGA battlestations on social media, this era- and Trumpism- are all but dead and buried.

comments.name: Steve M
comments.body: Happy we have all become a bit wiser from this experience (I hope) but wondering if these three will return to DC to see out their terms or will they just turn their back on their constituents and stay home?

articles.title: Three MAGA Women Who Defined an Era in Congress Are Exiting
articles.summary: Representatives Marjorie Taylor Greene, Lauren Boebert and Nancy Mace embodied a combative, attention-seeking brand of politics that defined the Republican Congress.

comments.name: Mr. Bentley
comments.body: I am paying a quarter of a million dollars and mortgaging my life to "learn" something I already learned in high school?

comments.name: Sara P
comments.body:
I hate the argument of “it will prepare you for the working world to know how to use AI.”  Most AI is developed and presented in a way that eliminates almost all barriers to use, allowing the dumbest people you know to use it. Sure, if you want to use it to make an automation tool that can scan incoming charges across an org for a day and sort them based on class of charge, you need some education. But that is not at all the type of AI being used in colleges, so it’s a moot point. 

If anything, the last couple groups of hires who went to school while AI was available are weaker at knowledge retention and problem solving, and can’t do anything without AI. So learn to use your brain on your own - that is what will really distinguish you in the working world. And when AI fails to live up to its promise, you can join me as one of the few people left who can do their job just fine without AI.

comments.name: David Wald
comments.body: I am 75 years old. I use Google AI all the time to get information and actually have somewhat intellectual conversations with it at times! My main concern about the use of AI in education is that I think that students will not learn how to write and make arguments through their writing if they rely on it to do so. I guess AI is okay for getting information, but young students will not get all that satisfaction out of roaming the library stacks!!!

comments.name: Spock
comments.body: This is like the blacksmiths who refused to learn how to forge pistons because they wanted to be in the horseshoe business.

comments.name: boomshaka
comments.body: Sundar Pichai's family must be allowed to hear what school parents want to say, every single day of their lives for the number of hours that kids stay on their Google AI search.

comments.name: Steven
comments.body:
This kind of thinking reminds me of medieval churches banning the teaching that the sun is the center of the solar system. Or banning the teaching of Darwinism. 

How ridiculously closed minded. How about we ban electricity, radio, television, computers, airplane travel, genetic engineering. 

You know, many came out against bicycles when they were first invented in the 1800s afraid that they can take children miles away from their homes in minutes!

AI is a valuable information source, it’s a tool - it doesn’t replace analysis or critical thinking.

comments.name: Douglas
comments.body:
I encourage you all to watch an interview from just a few days ago by the well-known AI podcast Dwarkesh, as he interviews an Open AI Board member named Paul Christiano who is a research expert.

You can easily find this on Youtube too. Christiano says we are on a pace to develop Super intelligence in the next year! Christiano is extremely frightened of what this will mean and believes AI development should pause until it could be made safe. 

This is one of the most terrifying interviews I’ve ever heard or seen. It really drove home for me how we are very likely in a matter of months to have catastrophe. After watching this interview I began calling every single U.S. Senator’s office pleading with them to stop AI development now!

Please do the same.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body:
By the way…see the next story down, the one about Anthropic’s gigundo IPO?

That’s what AI’s about. Got zip to do with teaching kids.

articles.title: The Anti-A.I. Campus Movement Is Growing
articles.summary: Some students are refusing to use A.I., and others are starting petitions to limit it across entire campuses. Colleges have taken notice.

comments.name: Pete
comments.body: Replacing USAID and trying to help in Sudan are worthy, long-term goals, but if they use political capital on anything but domestic priorities, especially initially, they will not be in the majority for long.

articles.title: ‘It’s Easier Said Than Done’: 3 Opinion Writers on How to Check Trump
articles.byline: Massimo Calabresi, David French, Lydia Polgreen and Stephen Stromberg
articles.summary: Presidents usually have wide latitude on foreign policy. Will the next Congress change that?

comments.name: Tim Fotinos
comments.body:
Is it possible to create a sand-box sort of game that develops a GT following with out any violence? Or, at least, nor glorifying guns?

We don't want a game that is just real life on a screen. There needs to be something interesting happening.  Better yet, interesting, visually and audibly rich, with significant choices for interaction, and multiple paths to more advanced quests.
And different paths using different skills, eye-hand, OR puzzle solving, OR debate skill, OR organizing projects, OR entrepreneurship, OR creativity...

I doubt we'll ever know.

comments.name: mikelew
comments.body: Wow! What an outstanding writeup both for gamers and non gamers. Bonus points for explaining how changes to society altered the the game's load-bearing funhouse mirror.

comments.name: Dave O
comments.body: A thought-provoking read. What happens when the reality and the simulacra can't be distinguished? I'm reminded of the creators of "Veep" remarking that their show as political parody couldn't compete with actual political reality. Young people have been dealt a rawer deal than previous generations and most can't imagine the milestones of living in the city, or having kids, or buying a house. Political institutions are at best, indifferent, and at worst, adversarial. The fantasy for them is American dream. This satirical take on our current capitalism run-amok existence sounds to me like an old-fashioned good time.

comments.name: AM
comments.body: I’ve had a chance to play for several hours today and because of my dad’s work I grew up for a while in the part of the world where this game is set around interesting sorts of people some of whom weren’t wildly dissimilar from the background characters in the story and this thing is nothing short of amazing. I feel like I’m a kid again in a boatyard watching the sun go down out over the water or peering through the car windshield while we cross a bridge or causeway in a downpour under a low grey sky. It’s crazy. I am truly staggered.

comments.name: MTX
comments.body:
I'm not really a gamer, and I hope this question doesn't come across as weird or even  condescending, but I really don't get it.

Why does this, especially the launch, mean so much to people?  It's entertaining, sure, but there seems to be no tribal aspect like with sports teams.  There seems to be no real accomplishment by the gamer. Not that there needs to be, if course.  Why then does this mean so much to me?

Is this somehow similar to people camping out in front of Apple stores?  That's also something that I never really "got", and I can't even guess if it's the same kind of thing or not.

So... what exactly is this about?

comments.name: Keith Tarzana
comments.body:
Having read only bad press of GTA in its early years, I never imagined a day would come that I might enjoy reading about the latest iteration. Some passages escape me, but his primary audience is aficionados, and I'm sure they get the jokes.

Thank you, Joseph Bernstein. And I guess Rockstar officials, who gave him time to absorb and write about the new game.

comments.name: Jon
comments.body: I don't want to stare at a screen any more than absolutely required for work,  paying bills,  etc. It feels like torture.

comments.name: John
comments.body: Within the last year a man was walking down a major street in our small city randomly shooting at passing cars. GTA style.  In a nearby metro area a man was randomly running down pedestrians with his car. GTA style. In several places nationwide people have driven into crowds of people.  GTA style.  I can't help but compare the actions of some ICE agents to the GTA game.  So does the game follow our culture or is our culture influenced by video games. Both I suppose.  Maybe we need to separate those who want to be in a position of power by those that play violent video games and those that don't.  Is or was Hegseth a video game player? He seems simple minded enough to let himself be influenced by such games.  This makes me think that the best candidates for important public positions are now women who are more likely to not play violent video games.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto Used to Satirize American Life. Now We’ve Caught Up With It.
articles.summary: The G.T.A. series is more than just a crime simulator — it’s a cartoonish sendup of our country. What happens when reality outruns the joke?

comments.name: John of Roncesvalles
comments.body: In a few years, AI will perfect capitalism so that the economy is no longer cyclical.

comments.name: William
comments.body: The world is tumbling into oblivion under an avalanche of AI billionaires untaxed billions, and no one seems concerned. Congress, irrespective of which party is in control, will not bite this particular hand, even after a voter mandate driven in part at least by concerns of data centers. Much like big oil of the past, AI has signaled a willingness to sacrifice any and everyone before loss of return on investment. This is an existential threat and people should begin to treat it as such. Hyperbole? I don't think so. As Henry Kissinger is reported to have quoted, "Just because you are paranoid does not mean someone isn't out to get you."

comments.name: Theodore Schleifer
comments.body: Ten years ago, I wrote my first piece about Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, a bit player in the movie “The Social Network” who was bursting onto the scene politically to try and take on Trump. I didn’t think I would still be writing about him a decade later, but here we are. I find him one of the most fascinating characters in Silicon Valley, politics and philanthropy — and today’s story is just one into why.

comments.name: Smilodon7
comments.location: Gilead, State Formerly Known As Missouri
comments.body: He’s worried about this?  He’s not the one likely to lose his livelihood.  I’m at a hard to find a job age even without AI.  I could easily find myself with no income at the time of my life when I should be making the most.  I’m supposed to do what?  Retrain at 57 -  For what?  Who is going to hire someone who will be over 60 by the time retraining finishes?

comments.name: AV
comments.body: Anthropic and AI technology is certainly worthy of extensive and deep coverage, but I am not sure why this IPO stuff is so interesting? After a certain point the number of zeros is not that relevant. I think the lionizing of the zeros is part of the problem.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body: Something as dangerous as AI in the hands of shareholders. There's only one way this ends, and it's not going to be happy.

comments.name: Bob
comments.body: Today is another of those days where retirees, or those with investment accounts designed to carry them into retirement, lose confidence in the market’s volatility. It’s a total shell game which benefits the insiders and holds the rest of us hostage to IPO’s, profit takers, and outright fraudsters. Do you ride it out, or look for a way to get out safely without chasing losses?

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body: I’m listening to your concerns Mr. Moskovitz. Unfortunately my voice does not contain enough zeros backing it up for anyone to care much about my opinion. Please do keep speaking out as you indeed have the requisite zeros necessary to be heard here in the land of the free (market). Thanks for your efforts.

articles.title: One of Anthropic’s Biggest I.P.O. Winners Feels a Bit Uneasy About the Whole Thing
articles.summary: An early investment that Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz made in Anthropic is paying off. But it’s not making him happy.

comments.name: altecocker
comments.body:
Econ 101:
The supply of X commodity (e.g. housing) remains steady
The demand for X commodity (e.g. housing) goes up
The invisible hand of the marketplace says the price MUST rise

comments.name: Jewell Firestone
comments.body: Well, based on past experience, they won't spend it on San Francisco culture. They won't buy art or go to art galleries. They won't go to music shows featuring Bay Area artists. They won't connect with makers at street fairs. They won't donate money to any of the hundreds of genuinely altruistic NGOs that serve Bay Area families. They will quietly walk past all of that smiling meekly in their Patagonia vests and sensible Sketchers, each step yielding compounding returns on their unearned wealth.

comments.name: Poo-poo point
comments.body:
It is so depressing to hear about another chunk of tech workers making out with insane (for everyone else) amounts of money. This kind of inequality has nothing good to offer society at large.
Living in Seattle I watch tech transform the Seattle economy, the tech worker/consumers live comfortable lives, and outsource their domestic labor to underpaid service workers (baristas, nannies, Lyft drivers etc). There are two Seattles— one that can do almost anything they want, and one that is more and more constrained by persistent financial limitations.  It’s discouraging that our national mythology—that wealth is deserved and earned and poverty is a marker of poor moral character—some how persists when it’s so painfully obvious, over and over, that wealth is an unearned confluence of privilege, luck, public assistance and a state which refuses to adequately tax high income earners. Leaving us all impoverished by a deeply unequal society of takers and the taken from. Blegh.  I do think the cover images conveys some of this dystopian doomerism for me. So plus one for that.

comments.name: Kay
comments.body: What has been occurring over the past 25 years since I moved to the Bay Area is the diminishing of racial diversity in SF. And since the majority of those working in tech are far from being diverse, there are few black and brown newly minted rich tech workers purchasing homes, raising kids, and settling down in SF. Why not encourage people to stay local/ invest local - not just through a huge one time donation, but through investing in the residents.

comments.name: Mike B.
comments.body: I’m sure some will use their newfound wealth to go into politics because nothing encourages one’s delusions of civic capability like being really wealthy.

comments.name: Mr basilico
comments.body:
Congratulations to them. What they will likely do is buy all the houses in the region in all-cash transactions. 

The public servants in the Bay Area who have been saving for a down payment on a home should start looking at other parts of the country because this one is simply out of reach.

comments.name: SoCalRocks
comments.body: What will Anthropic workers do with their wealth in the Bay Area? Do what they've always done:  Make life even more unaffordable in San Francisco and the surrounding areas.

comments.name: D. Smith
comments.body:
Yet another article evidencing the desperate need in this country to encourage research, innovation and hard work without minting arrogance and entitlement built from outlandish wealth. Do these people deserve extraordinary rewards? We still do not know or fully understand the value of AI so the jury is out. But we do know the potential moral hazard and unintended consequences of excessive wealth, not to mention the basic economic realities of the uber wealthy competing against each other to drive prices up so everyone else cannot afford a place to live or a decent meal.

By all means give these folks life changing bonuses, but the black swan wealth achieved through stock options needs to be curbed, not encouraged to the detriment of the many equally talented and hardworking people who are not fortunate enough to ride the coattails of the relatively few companies that hit it big.

articles.title: The Bay Area Wonders: What Will Anthropic Workers Do With Their Wealth?
articles.summary: San Francisco isn’t preparing for an Anthropic shopping spree after employees gain newfound affluence from the company’s initial public offering.

comments.name: Laura
comments.body:
Librarian I like to cut to the chase.

"I see that you are trying to be quiet, but your whispers are not as quiet as you think they are. Can you take your phone calls somewhere else? I find them distracting. Thanks."

She'll probably argue and deflect, and you'll smile at her and if necessary bring her back to the point. "Thanks for telling me that it's annoying how I staple loudly. I can staple out in the hall as well. We can just keep the noisy stuff out there."

As to the amount of time she is on the phone and not working, unless that is impacting your work or you are going to be held to account, I wouldn't worry about it.

comments.name: Annie
comments.body: Keep Thanksgiving a time to cherish family. Set aside another time when everyone can gather with the father and his doctor and or a social worker to plan out his care. This is a big talk that doesn't need to spoil a holiday meal.

comments.name: Barbara
comments.body: It would be nice to keep Thanksgiving as a happy memory so avoiding this Big Talk would be good. However, it is important that your husband and his sisters do have that talk with their father. Perhaps they could decide amongst themselves exactly what kind of help they think he needs now and how they would provide it, emphasizing that this comes from love rather than a need to control. Once they know what they want to do, then they could all visit their father together and discuss it with him. I have no personal experience with Alzheimer's, but understand how difficult it is for all involved. Good luck.

comments.name: Rocky
comments.body: You don’t need help because this isn’t about you.  There are bigger issues at play here than your vision of Thanksgiving dinner (which you may view as a reflection of yourself as a person).  Your job is to just be a part of the experience, nothing more.  Your husband’s job (which he has incorrectly assumed to be) is to waylay his father at an inconvenient time with the hopes of the immediate and extended family providing support.  Shame on him.  What would be his reaction if this tactic were used on him?

comments.name: BJ
comments.body: It's unclear why a fraught discussion about care for a parent with Alzheimer's must take place adjacent to or during a holiday meal.  The idea of framing it as freeing the father to do other things may help, but asking the father what he would like to do in the future as his illness progresses may be more productive.  It could also lead to recognition that now is the time to begin to institute appropriate changes so that all is in place as time goes on.

comments.name: RM Chicago
comments.body:
"My husband and I are hosting Thanksgiving this year, and my husband wants to lay down the law with his father and insist that the siblings be allowed to take greater control of his care. I wish this weren’t happening at the holiday, but I’m trying to be supportive. How do I host a joyful Thanksgiving amid sad news?"

There's never really a good time for conversations like this.  If everyone will be together in-person for Thanksgiving, and as it's always better to deal with these issues sooner rather than later, then Thanksgiving time is when the conversation should happen.  But, instead of focusing on the timing of the conversation, it would be better to focus on the substance of the conversation, making sure the messages are conveyed to the father-in-law in a way he understands and is more likely to accept.  It might be helpful for the husband and sisters to confer with an expert on these situations before speaking with their father.

comments.name: storm
comments.body:
the response to Librarian is funny, thinking that everyone actually does their work at their jobs. it's frankly very possible that the LW's coworker is on their phone through the entire workday. which is a separate issue, if she's not actually doing her job; the annoyance her phone calls are causing is probably the least of the issue.

For Son, I suspect your dad probably knew what was in the photo negatives when he shared them. I don't think the conversation is going to be as fraught as LW thinks it is.

comments.name: Dana
comments.body: LW1-How exactly is the husband going to "lay down the law"?  Has a judge determined his father to be legally incapacitated in any way?  If not, then the father retains all decision making rights.

articles.title: My Husband Is Planning a Hard Talk With His Father at Thanksgiving. Help!
articles.summary: A reader asks whether there’s any way to keep a conversation about her father-in-law’s worsening Alzheimer’s disease from torpedoing her plans for a joyful holiday.

comments.name: Bkes
comments.body: honestly wonder how this one will go, maybe the most consequential IPO of the era

comments.name: Graeme
comments.body: But it released only about 5.5% of its stock.   There's some gamesmanship in these small percentage vs big "value" partial floats

comments.name: Rev B
comments.body: Retiring in just over three months.  Hoping for the best, but I know how to hunt and dress game.  My wife gardens very successfully.  Plan B I place.

comments.name: Baron95
comments.body:
It's truly amazing how "anti-AI" the comment sections of the NYT are.

It can only possibly be coming from those who do not use AI on a daily basis, and formed their opinions under the assumption that AI meant the hallucination-prone chatbots of 2023.

I couldn't do my work nearly as well, running a brand new start up company, without AI. My daughter could not do hear work as an engineering college student nearly as well, without AI.

AI is a *huge* multiplier of our intelligence and skills, in virtually any field. My personal trainer is a top competitive body builder and AI has transformed his training, nutrition, and client practice completely. We still move the weights, but we now do it much more closely to optimally. 

And we are basically in year 3 of modern AI. Can you imagine year 5? (maybe). Year 10? (no one alive will recognize the world). The possibilities are incredible. And AI-enhanced security, AI-enhanced privacy, AI-enhanced safety, will all be a part of it.

Cars will be safer. Planes will be safer. Medicines will be safer. IT-infrastructure will be safer. AI is supercharging the future. 

Those who feared the printing presses, the Internet, will of course fear AI. But at least be sufficiently informed by using it.

comments.name: michjas
comments.body: This IPO reveals that there is still great confidence among investors in AI. It’s like magic. Nvidia stock tanks and lots of that money moves to Anthropic.  The bubble lives on for another day.  And I suspect that most of those who recognize the down side of AI nonetheless haven’t moved their money out of AI and into pork bellies.

comments.name: Mr. DeBeer
comments.body: The Nvidia chips that produced this wealth are made in Taiwanese factors by Filipino contract workers with  no power to determine the conditions under which they work, to organize for a fair wage, and to share in any of the wealth they are producing.  This is the essence of unregulated Capitalism.

comments.name: Pelasgus
comments.body: Fictitious value stoked by Federal deficit spending.

comments.name: Billy Wib
comments.body: Truly amazing what it can do, but equally truly amazing how we lack an ability to understand how it truly works or what it means long-term to continue this way, but let it rip? YOLO

articles.title: Anthropic Sells $81.3 Billion Worth of Shares in World’s Largest I.P.O.
articles.byline: Erin Griffith, Lauren Hirsch and Cory Weinberg
articles.summary: The sale valued the A.I. company, which makes the Claude chatbot, at more than $1.5 trillion. Shares begin trading on Thursday.

comments.name: roaxle
comments.body: This is exactly why I subscribe to the NY Times! I wish everybody did.

comments.name: San Sam
comments.body:
This piece, along with the recent report: “How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military” show some of the most frustrating aspects of your reporting on Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Specifically, the question posed in a NYTimes headline days ago (“Is China Buying Banned Nvidia Chips?”) is still unanswered.  Also unanswered is whether chips have been smuggled into China, because “buying” isn’t the same as “smuggling.”

Even in this current piece, these answers are not provided. Instead, we only read of “the possibility that banned, high-end Nvidia chips were smuggled into China.”

“We have not definitely established that Alice Huang was a spy.”  You certainly write as if she is.  The assumption that she was a spy appears to be based on the idea that she is an accomplished Chinese businesswoman (and maybe that is enough, although it means that Chinese spies are everywhere).

Stories in the NYTimes about Nvidia invariably mix-up chips that are allowed to be sent to China, with more powerful chips that may not. Also, the stories invariably confuse the idea of China being “within reach” or having “access” to powerful chips in data centers in other countries (such as Johor, Malaysia) with the idea that the chips have been delivered to China. 

In your next piece, please explain how China is prevented from using data centers for its nefarious purposes when the data centers are located outside of China – say, in Virginia.

The words of Blaise Pascal are ringing in my mind--

--and sorry!  I can't give them in French.  

"The eternal silence of those infinite spaces frightens me."  

The more so--

--because that quantity of empty space is literally unimaginable.  I cannot visualize it.  I cannot comprehend it.  

But there it is.  And these two Voyager crafts!  The heart beats faster.  As I recall the lines of Emily Dickinson.  

                      "This is my letter to the world
                            That never wrote to me."  

Hey, universe!  This is our letter to you.  These tiny things are laden with stuff that might bring to your attention--

--that fact that we live on a planet teeming with life and light! 

--that we are human beings--

--that human beings do things, suffer things--

--and, above all, accomplish things--

--as witness these two tiny things hurtling on and on--

--into an immeasurable blackness.  Into the dark--

--into the silence.  

Thanks, NYT.

comments.body: HEALTHSPAN seems a much better goal than lifespan to this old-timer. I recently relocated, shortly after my 80th birthday, to a not-for-profit continuing care residential community near my retirement home in western NC. My main motivation was that I had a lot of chronic health issues with high risk for heart attacks and strokes plus several injuries related to falls and bad reactions to lipid-lowering meds. One could argue that the latter was an example of good intentions gone bad in health care, but considering that I have a family history of early death from heart attacks plus needing three-vessel bypass surgery at age 60 due to elevated lipids, sugar, and blood pressure, after which I enjoyed 15 years of mountain hiking without cardiac symptoms, I'm resigned to a limited life-span if I can keep active and sane. Looking around me, I have plenty of examples of elderly folks who seem rather pleasant-tempered but whose lives are so complicated by various disabilities that I wouldn't trade places with them for another ten years of longevity. It does seem that numerous shady operators are attempting to profit from our fear of falling into senescence, but the profit motive has led America into world leadership in quality of life generally, so I'm not ready to trade that for a broken budget crisis and medical mediocrity even though I don't expect to continue my healthspan indefinitely. comments.name: Blandino

I bought a 4-unit property for $92K in a "bad" neighborhood in Berkeley in 1983 because I was 44 and needed to stop renting, but couldn't afford a single-family home.  (Adjusting for inflation, that purchase price equals $315K in today's dollars.)

It was relatively cheap because Berkeley had enacted a rent control law in 1980 and older landlords were dumping and fleeing, as has happened in NYC.

It was a major struggle at first, supporting it with a fulltime job and a diet of peanut butter sandwiches, but even with minimal allowed increases, inflation gradually eased my situation, and when I sold it in 2015 at age 75 it was for over a million.  

All in all, I have to say I support rent control.  It made my purchase possible, and though it made my life harder when I was young it has made my last years comfortable.

I don't think people understand inflation, and I'm not entirely sure I do.

But consider this:  I had $80K in a money market at 1% and decided to put it into the stock market in 2022.  That investment is now at $93K, which sounds great until you adjust for inflation.  It turns out that my $93K is only worth $78K in 2022 dollars.  Of course, if I'd left it in a money market it would have grown to only $83.5K, which equals $70.2K today.

That's 12.5% inflation in four years, during which my $80K nest egg would have deflated to $70K in a money market account.

My point is that rental real estate remains a gold mine for owners.  Don't pity them.

Nor should we allow the system to make landlords poorer with each passing year.

Rent control, one-sided laws that disproportionately favor tenants, rising operating expenses, and the substantial costs of maintaining aging buildings all undermine the economic incentives to invest in rental housing. Without a reasonable balance between the rights and interests of tenants and landlords, investment capital will inevitably seek opportunities elsewhere.

Unless the City adopts more equitable policies that recognize the legitimate interests of both parties, its older, rent-restricted buildings will continue to deteriorate, potentially becoming uninhabitable. At the same time, investment in new housing will increasingly flow to cities that welcome and encourage investment rather than penalize it. The result will be less investment, a declining supply of affordable rental housing, and an even more severe housing crisis.

If the allegations are substantiated, his conduct would represent an appalling breach of responsibility and an unacceptable disregard for America’s national security interests. His apparent pursuit of enormous profits for his company must never be allowed to take precedence over the security of his country.

The seriousness of these allegations demands a thorough investigation and accountability, regardless of his wealth, influence, or position as the former CEO of one of the world’s most prominent chipmakers. No individual should be above the law simply because he happens to be a billionaire or a celebrated technology entrepreneur.

Considering the gravity of the allegations and the serious national security concerns surrounding this affair, Nvidia’s Board must remain resolute in its decision not to reinstate Jensen Huang, regardless of any pressure or lobbying from influential business associates or political figures. The sign was also tatty and in great need of repair. We were also the only ones there on a weekday and I don’t recall seeing too many residences nearby. 
Of course things change in twenty years and everything a traveler could peaceably enjoy once is now overrun by tourists doing it for the gram. 
It’s happening at the Hollywood sign, it’s happening in Central Park, it’s happening in Seattl and Amsterdam and Barcelona. And I don’t see a solution until we start to prioritize the primary experience we have with our eyes, ears and other senses over using the phone to reproduce cliched simulacra to be chance our status and get those all important likes.

comments.body: Many public lands (both federal and state) restrict access and have resorted to a reservation system. Perhaps a timed entry reservation system is needed together with no parking and immediate towing  near the site. A free or inexpensive shuttle bus could be provided  for visitors and residents with reservations.   A clear viewing are should then be provided and maybe a hiking trail.  A guide could be provided.  Other than that folk would be required to walk from legal parking (no Ubers taking you to the site).  Just an idea that has worked other places

comments.name: Stephen Schlaudt
comments.body:
I live adjacent to a small pubic access to a lake. The lane I live on is a private dirt road with absolutely no place to turn around. During summers, mostly on weekends, but continuously in July and early August access to the private lane is completely blocked by cars stopping to unload people, kayaks, and tubes. The parking and beach are free therefore attracting tourists and local water enthusiasts from cities more than an hours drive away. The issues are obvious to anyone with experience with crowded public accesses. Complete disregard for private property owners rights and safety, damage to property, dangerous driving and behavior, garbage and filth. As long term residents of the area we have managed to control the most dangerous situations and to keep our families safe, and avoid aggressive interactions. The most common issue is a lack of enforcement by local police, and a failure to respond to the residents and the public when required. We are not elites attempting to limit access to public spaces. The public needs to be under self control or the authorities have an an absolute responsibility to enforce compliance with the laws.
Stephen

comments.name: BJ
comments.body:
I was a social worker who was called upon to make such decisions. A paramount consideration should be the best interest of the children. Not just the time a parent spends on them, but the quality of the time, the values this parent encourages and the affection given to the children.  

It's usually best for children to be able to have relationships with both parents. Domestic abuse would be an exception, but otherwise, the more love children receive the better. They need both parents as they grow up.

comments.name: Cheez Leweez
comments.body:
What you should do is decide what's best for the kids, and act accordingly. Keeping in mind not creating more discord in their family is important. Is the difference in parenting so wide that it outweighs the stress you will cause by actively taking sides?

Divorce is not a horserace. As long as there are children involved, the family will still be an entity. Nevermind which parent is "better." Is one parent's involvement harmful to the children?

Hopefully, divorce and custody aside, both parents will stay involved with their children. Barring actual abuse, that's what's best for them in the long run.

comments.name: Anita
comments.body:
The letter writer's "opinion" about her daughter's parenting is just that-- an opinion-- and it's a very sexist one at that. For centuries fathers have been the ones working hard to provide financially for their children/families and they have not and should not be deprived of their parental rights or called bad fathers for doing so! Yet just because this mother's daughter works long hours at a stressful jobs, she thinks she should be?!

She doesn't see her daughter with her children because she is helping BOTH her daughter and son-in-law out by babysitting the grandchildren while they are presumably BOTH doing other things--and in the daughter's case, it's providing financially for the family. Either the son-in-law is doing the same thing while the grandma babysits, in which case she has a sexist double standard, or he is off doing other things, in which case, perhaps the daughter is the "better" parent for actually working to provide for the family. Or perhaps they are BOTH good parents. The letter writer really has no clue and should mind her own business and I think it's sad that she wants to butt in and hurt her daughter.

I think she is a bad mother who should be deprived of HER "rights"/opportunities to see her daughter and grandchildren. With a "mother" like that, who would need enemies? I hope the daughter finds out how awful her mother views her and distances herself and her children from her.

My child is also thriving, happy, has the ability to pursue his interests and passions, and loves me. 1. Unless grandmama has seen either parent abuse the grandchildren, she needs to mind her own business.  

2. Sometimes grown people have to choose the job that pays the bills. That is life. 

3. Sometimes one parent is a better parent. And it doesn't automatically mean that the other parent is bad. That, too, is life. 

4. Whenever possible, children should be raised by both parents. Or at least have 2 people actively involved in parenting them. 

5. Why does Mom hate Dad, is the bigger question.

comments.name: ILoveWine

There is a difference I have learned, between "custody" and "parenting time" Where I live in Canada anyway. The term custody is not used any more - rather it is called "decision making" and in a perfect situation both parents share it equally. Then there is the primary parent (who the child lives with the majority of the time) with the other parent having access as dictated by the situation regarding location, employment etc etc. 
The main factor concerning the court should be the best interests of the child, and  most of the time that is enjoying time with both parents equally. 
I don't think you should get involved at all - except as a supportive and concerned third-party.

In the small lake community where I spend the summer, along with mostly year-rounders, we practice this without really thinking about it. Perhaps once a summer a storm brings power lines down. Some have generators that kick in automatically, others crank up a portable, others have none, So some of us share what we can in freezer space, portable lighting etc. Also the well pumps go out so we have to fill toilet tanks by hand. If a tree comes down across the road, It's usually only minutes before two or three neighbors are out with chain saws, and team up for safety. Some go without internet for the duration, in one case two whole days. It's not armageddon, but it does provide a certain amount rehearsal for community, and reminds everyone to keep water, and an extra five or ten gallons of gasoline in their shed. 

Meanwhile, there are places here in the USA, and around the world, where people are surviving trauma and deprivation every day, like building collapses, wildfires, floods, earthquakes, mad gunmen, drone strikes, foreign invaders, and missile attacks.

I am grateful for my good fortune and count my blessings.

The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law is delivering transformational results across the Northeast Corridor—from the new Portal North Bridge and the Frederick Douglass Tunnel in Baltimore to the rehabilitation of the East River Tunnels and a revitalized Penn Station. These historic investments prove what is possible when we commit to rebuilding the backbone of American rail.

​Yet as we construct the new Hudson River Tunnels, we must look beyond the Manhattan core and ask a vital question: how do we ensure this generational investment reaches the outer-borough communities that need economic and transit opportunity the most? By integrating commuter railroads and intercity rail services across the region, we can give travelers faster, more direct links to our major airports while relieving congestion across our busiest transit hubs.

​Rather than settling for a standalone light rail system like the Interborough Express (IBX), we should establish a direct heavy-rail connection from the LIRR Main Line into the LIRR Bay Ridge Branch. Leveraging existing Class 1 rail infrastructure to bring full commuter and intercity rail service directly into the heart of Brooklyn and Queens would deliver faster speeds, higher capacity, and seamless one-seat or cross-platform transfers—connecting historically underserved neighborhoods to the entire Northeast Corridor and unlocking true regional equity for generations to come.

In 2026, researchers using DNA language models like Evo 2 and Omnii demonstrated how AI can design custom bacteriophages, while scientists built predictive models that map how genetic mutations disrupt RNA splicing. By narrowing millions of genetic possibilities down to viable lab candidates in days rather than years, this research gives doctors new tools against antibiotic-resistant infections and spares families with rare diseases years of agonizing diagnostic guesswork.

Climate scientists and mathematicians at New York University (with NVIDIA) released models in 2026, open-source AI ocean-atmosphere emulators that simulate up to 4,000 years of ocean and El Niño patterns in a single day on one standard GPU. Because that kind of forecasting previously required a multimillion-dollar supercomputer only wealthy nations could afford, local towns and universities anywhere can now test sea-level defenses and protect crops on a modest budget.

At the July 2026 AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva, UNESCO and the Coalition for Sustainable AI recognized winners of the Resilient AI Challenge, where research teams compressed open-source text, speech, and image models to slash energy use while preserving accuracy. Directly addressing concerns over power-hungry data centers, this work makes reliable translation, transcription, and educational tools usable in areas with limited power grids without straining local energy supplies or driving up utility bills.

But as far as Russia’s strategic calculations go, it is irrelevant what the West is spending its dwindling finances on - air defences or damage repairs in Ukraine - the cost is the cost and all money are the same. In terms of economics and cost structure of this war Russia has an enormous advantage which Europe cannot reduce no matter how hard it tries. comments.body:
While I cheer the destruction of half of the Kerch bridge, and hope that Ukraine will soon also destroy the rail bridge, I also fear that Ukraine is now one significant step closer to being nuked or gassed by a thoroughly humiliated and vengeful Putin, who may no longer be able or willing to resist the calls of his super-nationalist elites to conclude the Ukraine War quickly and decisively.

Russia knows that Ukraine will be exceedingly difficult to defeat with conventional weapons, and that continued ground operations will be extremely costly and bloody.  Moreover, unless the Zelensky Government is toppled, just seizing more land won't stop the conflict, which is likely to mutate into an extremely bloody insurgency carried on by what remains of Free Ukraine. Wars do not end until there is a complete military and political surrender, which Ukraine may be unwilling to do. Russia says that it is prepared to continue fighting for decades, yet there may come a point where Putin may be politically unable to continue the war. When that point is reached, he is quite likely to go for the Hiroshima Option, or alternatively conduct kinetic strikes against the Baltics, hoping to break NATO and force the EU to completely abandon Ukraine.

The greater Putin's humiliation and the longer the war drags on without the clear prospect of a crushing Russian victory, the greater the odds of a truly grisly escalation with unknowable consequences. What is certain is that Putin will not back down.

comments.name: AK
comments.body:
I've lived here in Miami since 1992.  It's a complex city, like any of its size, with dark undercurrents that rarely (if ever) seem to make it into a movie, tv show, book or video game for that matter.  There are talented and hard working people here.  Most are just trying to raise families and create a future for their kids.  But there's an odd ethic... and a lack of ethics.  Superficiality and envy are endemic.  
There is something very near to a caste system here.
It's deeply segregated involving extreme racial divides, particularly with the black population.  Think deep south with a Caribbean colonialist attitude.
Corruption exists everywhere in the world, but it's practically celebrated in Miami.  There's a quiet pride about it. The justifications I've heard smack of a deeply rooted sense of entitlement and being owed something.  If you don't agree, you simply don't understand (and you might be a communist).
Infrastructure is an afterthought.
While there are certainly conservationists here, the prevailing sentiment is that nature must be subdued.
Every man for himself.  Having moved here from another city 34 years ago, it seems the sense of community here is minimal and what does exist is often along cultural lines.

Miami's hope is continually reimagined.  All of the positive things about it are well promoted.  It's authenticity might prove disappointing to newly arrived.

But don't try to duplicate this in Sydney! The

But the glass was overwhelmed by a massive square ice cube, and maybe a tablespoon of vermouth just to the top of that ice cube. I sat there waiting for our host to come back with another bottle and continue pouring. Maybe they ran out? It was $16 AUD.  The hosts were Spanish! Seriously, they know who they are. comments.name: R Stuart
comments.body: Department store food halls, once a source of wonder, have dteriorated around the world - New York, Paris, Berlin, London - and are now mainly expensive pre-made dispensaries. El Cortes in Madrid has so far bucked the trend, with most stores having full grocery sections, with wonderful butchers, cured meats, hams, in addition to fresh fruit and vegetables.

comments.name: BBB
comments.body: We have been eating our way through South East Asia, Japan, and Australia for most of our adult lives, but we try to take long stays in Madrid on a regular basis. The markets are even more fun when you rent an apartment with well stocked kitchen tools. Upon arrival we first stop by the local El Cortes Ingles kitchenware department, pick up a new wheeled hand cart, and head straight to the markets. Once there we pile our treasures into our colourful new Rolser and take it back to our temporary kitchen and start cooking. You will find an abundance of perfect, fresh produce in these markets. But look closely at the highlighted photos of the plates on the tables. Few, if any, green vegetables. You will even struggle to find them in the Chinese restaurants as well! The Spanish cuisine does not feature a lot of green vegetables. But  the municipal markets spread out across the city are the best place to look for them.  Also visit  these fancy grocers: Sanchez Romero,  and the  Serrano branch of El Cortes Ingles in barrio Salamanca.

comments.name: Jason
comments.body: What this article misses (between traditional and Michelin-starred gastronomia molecular) is the vast middle register of cocina nueva (what we call farm to table and fusion in the US) restaurants in which you can get a fabulous, creative 3-course meal for 1/3 the Michelin prices. Google the name of the town (or in Madrid or Baecelona, the name of the neighborhood and “cocina de autor o de mercado” and you’ll get (in Madrid) dozens of fantastically varied choices, creative and delicious, rooted in local ways but lightened and mixed up for 40, 50, 70 or 90 euros a 3-course meal. The notion you have to choose between tapas and spherified deconstructions is especially silly in Madrid—with possibly now the most dynamic, international and diverse food scene on the planet IF you know how to inform yourself a little.

I can't relate to Galadriel being a plucky elf in her 20s who is racing around, sword in hand, and being adventurous. By the end of the second age she has to be at around 5000 years old. She would be a wise, stable, and mature adult not some ridiculous Generation whatever. 

And, Gandalf came in the 3rd age (year 1000). It's in Unfinished Tales and other works, including the appendix in LOTR. A few minor references Tolkien made about Gandalf maybe arriving for a bit in the 2nd age aren't enough to develop a story line.

This series would have been better set in the first age and the elves trying to retrieve the silmarils.

comments.name: Biker
comments.body: I've never read the source material. I Loved the first two seasons as they seemed to do a good job of drawing out the characters, their conflicts and the mysteries driving them. I'm enjoying the 3rd but it lacks the tension. Closest was whether the orc general was to be trusted...

comments.name: Gabriel
comments.body:
I read LOTR a dozen times at least, the Hobbit too, and the Silmarillion thrice or so. The latter was never as good a read, it’s more biblical and less of a character-focused narrative. But it’s good history for those of us who like the world Tolkien created. 

That being said, the three movies of The Hobbit were a slog that should’ve been reduced to about two hours in total. The Rings of Power, on other hand, is a decent and often fun depiction of the second age. Yes, some of the dialog is pretty horrid, but overall it’s visually stunning and a pleasant diversion for those of us who like to immerse ourselves in Middle Earth during our free time. (Particularly since it seems we might never get any more books in the Game of Thrones series. Yes, I’m throwing shade at you, George Martin.)

By comparison, is TROP as good as the first Star Wars trilogy (episodes 4 through 6)? No. But it’s probably ant least as good ans episodes 1 through 3. And much better than some of the SW spinoffs. 

I’m in for a penny, in for a pound.

comments.name: Eugene
comments.body: I often use critics as my bellwether to decide what to take a chance on. And I usually agree with them. But in this case, I disagree. I think the Rings of Power is great, and I’m a huge LOTR fan. I even took courses about it in college. I think both a new and classic vision can live side by side.

comments.name: Jxb
comments.body: I don’t not like RoP, but the first two seasons were static and saturated in a way that reliably lulled me into a stately sleep. And I mean that as a compliment—in this agitating time, having a show that helps you wind down is a beautiful thing. Most of the complaints here relate to the fact that this is true long form storytelling, which is rare on TV these days. Nowadays we just want to get to the fireworks factory. And the first two seasons did deliver a few of those moments, like the creation of Mordor and Mount Doom, just not enough for most. The third season seems to have heard this criticism and has sped up the storytelling in the manner of the later seasons of GoT. I’m enjoying it so far and hope it stays on the rails, unlike GoT. Again, I don’t dislike this show and want to see it succeed.

comments.name: Ovid
comments.body:
I stopped in the middle of episode 2 of season 1. From the first five minutes one can tell something is very wrong with it. Drawn out to a glacial pace, the dialogue is meaningless and has no point, as in the example James cited. And the identity politics were distracting to say the least. There was a 20 minute scene of a dwarf and his plus sized black dwarf wife just talking over dinner that was baffling, and it dawns on one that the show creators have no idea where they're going with all this. 

I read that each season costs Bezos about $500 million, but to cancel the series would only cost him $20 million termination fee. I wonder why he keeps spending $500 million on another season. Wheel of Time seasons 2 and 3 were incredible: they should have kept that show going and canceled this Rings of Power.

comments.name: Uncommon Sense
comments.body:
Sigh. So many tries at adapting JRR Tolkien’s legendarium to the screen. And so many fails. And part of that may be that much of his prequel work was more scholarly world creating than telling engaging stories. 

Peter Jackson’s LOTR pulled it off, with three great films. Yet even those, like many screen adaptations of complex literary works, fell short in being true to the trilogy.  

And since the execrable Hobbit series of films, 
I’ve just given up on watching any of the recent  Tolkien adaptions. They’re an assault on my memory. 

To digress, now let’s see what the film version of The Magician’s Nephew will be like. IMO it is right after The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe as the best in CS Lewis’ Narnia canon. I greatly fear how it may be butchered.

comments.name: Mayor Jared Kraham
comments.body:
I spoke to the New York Times at length about this — the inherent challenges of maintaining century-old carousels, and Binghamton's commitment to preserving them for future generations. Unfortunately, my perspective on the carousels was not included. 
 
The issue of keeping our community’s carousels running is not a matter of local government prioritizing funding and maintenance — we are more than willing to spend what’s needed. The challenge lies in the scarcity of companies still in operation nationwide that deal with antique mechanical ride systems and artisan historic restoration. 

A carousel is equal parts art and amusement ride. In Binghamton’s case, add “historic artifact” to the mix. Every horse must be hand-painted within historic guidelines. Every mechanical part must be custom fabricated. The scarcity of this craftsmanship means unpredictable timelines and frequent delays. 

When a breakdown inevitably happens, our dedicated Parks Department employees work wonders, but they are not antique carousel technicians. Larger issues mean the City has to rely on a few outside vendors to travel in from hours away. With other carousel operators nationwide needing the same services, the wait time is rarely quick. 

Broome County’s carousels are monuments of civic pride that bring a warmth and nostalgia to residents who remember riding them as kids, and a responsibility to preserve that tradition for future generations.

comments.body: Having spent a good deal of my life there, I can attest that there are several areas of the city that are not only desirable, but can fit most people's wallets. Housing prices are good, with large, older houses that are comfy and spacious. Lots of parks, abundant beauty in the area, a thriving downtown, many cultural institutions, and the "Strip" is a great market area. The North Side used to be a pass through to the mills, but with the mills gone, has taken on a life of its own. Heading out the other direction is Lawrenceville, which has become a haven for younger people. Then there is the University area, with the Univ of Pittsburgh, Carnegie Mellon and Carlow College, as well as the Carnegie Library, Museum, concert hall, hospitals, Phipps Conservatory, Schenley Park and more. It's a great town, sometimes called, "little New York," because of the concentration of so much into a doable town with wonderful neighborhoods.

We ended up in the East End of the city and love it to this day.  The houses on the Northside are amazing and there is a church with these amazing Tiffany windows.  The history is what makes Pittsburgh unique. At one time it was the center of industry for the country and there are still many very wealthy people that live here.  I love the diversity of the city, though it is not as diverse as one would think.  What I truly love about the city is its cultural institutions and the people.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: The image of Pittsburgh as a very low-crime city presented in this story is mostly true, but over the past two years, increasingly over the past year, we have suffered from violence, including several shootings, by minority teenagers, mostly in the city's downtown areas and on the North Side. That problem is increasing, not decreasing.

comments.name: Clare
comments.body: This is a The Pitt article. I retired home to Pittsburgh last year, after almost 40 years in Arlington, VA. I saw the latter destroyed by developers--made unaffordable, overcrowded and turned into McMansionville.  In addition, many working people were forced out by developers, higher taxes, and a greedy county board not supporting true diversity. With development along the metro line and the arrival of places like Trump's favorite Cheesecake Factory, it was the beginning of the end. Remember Amazon HQs Two and those broken promises to the County? I do not want Pittsburgh to suffer the same fate. You can be sure that once Dr. Robby is no longer on the air, the fascination with Pittsburgh will disappear. Hopefully rich people won't relocate to the Burgh and destroy it in the meantime.

Electricity here routinely goes out at least once in the winter and once in the summer. Keep your pantry stocked, have physical can openers. A paper book of Shakespeare's sonnets usually keeps me happy for quite a while. No phone pings, no bothers. It's life as we used to know it, and that's fine.

comments.name: Leonard Pone
