comments.name: Patricia
comments.body:
Putin has never agreed to a ceasefire with Ukraine, partial or otherwise. His position is that a ceasefire would give Ukraine the opportunity to regroup and rearm. Why are we entertaining the position that Putin was ever willing to do this?

It's pretty evident that Putin is unwilling to negotiate any concessions. His position is that Ukraine should capitulate--that it should cede its fortification line in northern Donetsk, disarm unilaterally, no foreign troops would be allowed to provide security assurances, and that its elections be subject to a veto from Moscow. Putin wants Ukraine to be another Belarus.

comments.name: Jorge
comments.body:
The Russian leader invited European representatives to Moscow to discuss giving them a role in negotiations, if the Eurocrats can figure out who should represent them.  That is a good thing, at least potentially.

The core "uncertainty" in this as-yet-unscheduled confab is not whether Putin was "serious," but whether the Europeans can scrape together a unified proposal, anoint a negotiator, and demonstrate they are willing to offer anything serious enough to prompt Putin to cut a deal.

At this stage, the Europeans seem content to hide behind Trump's diplomatic coattails, grumpily blaming him for the lack of peace progress, yet never advancing any helpful proposal of their own or empowering Ukraine to press on to victory.

The Europeans are free riders on their own continental defense, and free riders even in diplomacy.  It is long past time for them to carry their own water.

Trump is right.  This bloody stalemate cannot be allowed to go on any longer.  After five years and a million casualties, it is clear that Russia will not quit, Ukraine cannot win, and that Europe is pushing Ukraine to sacrifice a generation of young men to no avail.  

"We will fight to the death of the last Ukrainian," seems to be their battle cry.

This strategy may stroke Europeans' sense of honor, but it makes little sense.  Why not give peace a chance?

comments.name: HLR
comments.body: Putin will dominate Ukraine by peace if not war, unless Americans demand that Trump provide intelligence and defensive missiles to Ukraine.

comments.name: Jerry
comments.body: Russia, aka Putin, will do what Russia wants to do.  Their word is worthless, not that ours is much better.  Our president has some deranged idea that Putin will be honest with him and nothing could be further from the truth.  I was stationed in West Germany when the Russians rolled into Czechoslovakia in the late 60's. That same mindset still rules in Moscow.  Europe is right to be on alert.

comments.name: RCarroll
comments.body: Putin has never had any intent to end his invasion of Ukraine.

comments.name: George M
comments.body: He is unable negotiate because he has nothing to negotiate with except full withdrawal.

comments.name: Eddie Torial
comments.body: Putin wasn’t going to negotiate anyway.  This is just a convenient excuse.  Possibly for internal consumption more than for international.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body:
Putin has a problem. 

He cannot stop this war for a couple of key reasons. Firstly, the Russian economy is completely reliant on the war now, when it ends the economy will be in free fall and secondly, Russia has to win, or at least capture the Dombas. Failure to do so will mean he would be ousted and probably killed.

The other real problem for Putin is that Ukraine has turned this war around and is winning. If Russia’s bombing campaign fails over the winter, then Ukraine will emerge stronger. Their capabilities are growing daily & Europe is ramping up their support. Putin is playing for time, banking on Trump’s continued support and the hope that Marie le Pen wins in the French elections, therefore vetoing EU support.

articles.title: After Bridge Attack, Putin Says He Will ‘Not Be Negotiating’ Ukraine Cease-Fire

comments.name: Julie
comments.body: Honestly, I’d want to be an influencer only if I could make a positive impact without losing myself trying to be liked. Having a platform would give me a chance to encourage people and speak about things that matter to me. Still, I wouldn’t want likes and followers to decide how I feel about myself. I’d rather be respected for being real than admired for pretending to have a perfect life. At the end of the day, staying true to myself would matter more than being famous.

comments.name: Angel Figueroa Jr.
comments.body: I don’t think I would like to be an influencer because it’s a lot of work and I wouldn't want to be hated and judged by people. But If I was an influencer I think I would make sports videos and review sports equipment. In my opinion I feel like to make a good social media personality you need to be energetic, funny, and I feel like you always have to keep up with videos and your fans.

comments.name: Tristan Tran
comments.body: If I was able to have 1 million followers on a platform I would take it. Although people says that people might recognize your face I will just not put on a face cam, as I want to create Minecraft SMP content witch doesn't require one at all. However I not just doing it for fun as the platform that I'm on pays me 700-1500 dollars per video if 50% of my followers watches it(I looked it up). Also even if I pay an editor for $100 per video I still make money. So if I can trade a 9-5 job with 1 million followers I would ABSOLUTLY trade it

comments.name: Vinny Blood
comments.body: Being an influencer would be the last occupation that I would take up because friends turn into props, laughter turns into a laugh track, and ingenious joy turns into programmed content. I could not stand to feel the need to constantly record beautiful moments, ruining moments by enforcing a superficial persona for my circle of friends, family, and myself. I am not disregarding the technological advancement of the camera. A moment captured out of wonder is beautiful; a life lived for the camera is a performance. Occasionally recording moments that you find captivating is not an inherently unacceptable behavior, but constantly recording to post to a massive public audience tends to drain the life of those around the influencer. While the granted fame of being an influencer may bring riches and status, I would not like to trade it for having to constantly uphold a performance wherever I go.

comments.name: Abdullah H
comments.body: I think that the stat that 4 out of 5 gen Z's would want to be a influencer rather than work a 9-5 job makes sense, because an influencer has more flexibility and freedom in a sense. For example, if someone worked as an accountant they would be doing similar things everyday, with a specified schedule. Meanwhile an influencer gets to plan out there own day. I personally, would want to be an influencer rather than work a 5-9 job, because I would be able to do what I want everyday, rather than follow a schedule.

comments.name: Yelena
comments.body: Constantly recording yourself to maintain a steady social status seems exhausting until you see the benefits. Posting your daily activities and hobbies for people to see online is an easy way to gain money in my opinion. Having a unique way of entertaining people makes you stand out. 1 million people supporting you already gives you a good impression on social media, plus with the good benefits from your supporters you can gain much money from it.

comments.name: Justin M
comments.body: Personally, I would not want to be an influencer. Just like the girl in the article, there is such a big commitment when it comes to being an influencer. Additionally, there’s no guarantee you’ll be successful. Assuming you are successful - which normally requires posting a lot of content - you’re putting yourself out there so much and you can’t just take back what you post. It’s out there forever. Furthermore, you’re sacrificing so much time that it would make it difficult to live a life especially if you were in college. Being an influencer would distract from the college experience and coursework. If I knew I would be successful, always enjoyed making content, and could live a normal life then I would be an influencer. Too many ifs. I would rather have a steady 9-to-5 job. More so because I want to get a steady job that I enjoy and there’s a higher chance of success in that than becoming an influencer. Finally, if I was a popular influencer, I wouldn’t want to get swarmed by strangers. Which would be unavoidable. In conclusion, becoming an influencer just seems too risky and time consuming to me.

comments.name: Faizyab
comments.body:
I can see why being an influencer is appealing: you get to turn something you genuinely enjoy like gaming, art, fashion, science, or even explaining homework into something other people connect with. The creative freedom and chance to build a community seem like the best parts.
But I wouldn't want my whole life to become content. If every meal, friendship, or bad day could be judged by strangers, it would be hard to know whether I was doing something because I liked it or because it might get views. There's also pressure to stay interesting all the time, even when real life is ordinary.
I'd rather have a small audience that actually cares about what I make than millions of followers who expect me to perform constantly. Influencing can be a great opportunity, but only if the creator stays in control of their life not the algorithm.

This line is the excuse many cheaters use for their duplicity. Doesn’t matter what your marriage looks like and how you feel about it, cheating shows a lack of integrity and empathy for others. comments.name: Sandra
comments.body: Anyone who has raised toddlers knows there is no room you can go into and close the door that they will not follow you. I no longer have any bathtubs in my house. If you are too weak or infirm to bathe alone you need a shower with a bench or chair.  In assisted care homes you will be showered while in a wheelchair—sometimes with two assistants not just one. Only in the movies do they perpetuate the myth that a wet, slippery adult can be lifted out of a bathtub safely.

comments.name: Dorothy
comments.body: As fresh water is becoming more and more scarce around the world, I am aghast at the thoughtless self-indulgence that these bathrooms represent among those able to afford stylish lifestyles.  Since when is wasting water considered necessary for "self care'?  The whole home decor business is not about good solid decision making for reasonable comfort and attractiveness at home, but about maximizing profit and encouraging "updating" every few years.  Who cares about all the damage done to ecological systems?

comments.name: Susan
comments.body: You don't need bigger. That's silly. You do need easy to clean (which means, no stand-alone tub hard to get behind). You also should consider a bidet toilet - exceptional upgrade; the other thing is good lighting.

comments.name: Elizabeth
comments.body: People I know with freestanding tubs tucked against walls admit they are a pain the neck to clean — sometimes literally. Getting behind them is difficult, and you often need a squeegee or a sponge on a long stick. If it’s in a corner, good luck.

comments.name: Michelle
comments.body: Hilarious. I just ‘updated’ my bathroom by painting it earlier this year. As long as it’s clean and in working order that’s all I need. And my original tub from 1916 is still just fine. Go buy yourself some nice towels and be done with it.

comments.name: Westchester Peach
comments.body: My life changed once we renovated with double sinks in our bath. It’s not for everybody, I realize. But, that’s the most expansion I would care to do. Sauna, cold plunge, fridge, coffee station? No thanks.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body:
As someone who has renovated 15 bathrooms, some pushing 200sft, in various homes, I can say that personally, all these "spa-like" features were completely unused after the first month. Overhead rain shower? Nope. Body Sprays? Nope. Sauna? Nope. Steam Shower? Nope. Vessel sinks? Nope. Hand Showers? Nope. 

The only "fancy" thing I have in my current bathroom is a toilet/bidet combo. It's a first and I would do it again. 

I wonder how many people are like me, "It sounded good at the time..."

comments.name: Tallulah
comments.body: I've just remodeled my bathroom, to a cost of about $45K.  I had heated floors and a heated towel rack put in, as well as backlit mirror upscale tile and a walk in shower.   But I see no need for a lounge, a skin care refrigerator- I don't need a spa in my house.

comments.name: Liberty Apples
comments.body: The Biden administration came to the same conclusion long before this decision. The question now is whether the Trump administration will agree with this guilty verdict. There is nothing to suggest it will.

comments.name: Scott
comments.body: I'm a believer in effective instruments of global justice... but it took nine years for this court to make this ruling, clearly obvious to the rest of the world long ago, and there's no enforcement. Why would the world's bad actors care at all?

comments.name: slime2
comments.body:
A number of years ago, I was in Dublin and remember seeing a huge photo of Aung San Suu Kyi hanging from the side of a building, I guess in honor of her upcoming visit.

We now know, she deserved no admiration, no respect, and no recognition.  The only recognition she should receive now is a jail cell for the rest of her life.

comments.name: Susan
comments.body: We should welcome and honor the I.C.J. ruling, but I’m frustrated by its  snail’s pace internal mechanics, which allowed the ruling to take 10 years! International Humanitarian Law is a treasure of humanity, but it is practically meaningless if it takes a decade to deliver a ruling. Preventing genocide is futile if judicial rulings are delayed for years after the genocide occurred. That’s just common sense.

comments.name: Reasonable
comments.body: The key question in the legal determination of genocide is not the actual violence but the intent. The article states, “Thursday’s decision hinged on whether Myanmar acted with the specific intent to physically destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part, as an ethnic or religious group.” The likely reason that the vote was not unanimous is that proving intent is difficult; states committing genocide will obfuscate by making up other justifications.

comments.name: Giovanna
comments.body:
This might have been relevant in 2020, but this is a sideshow now. The same Tatmadaw that tried to purge the Rogingya have now killed 100,000 people and displaced over five million in its brutal civil war where crimes against humanity are daily occurrences. The Rohingya genocide barely scratches the surface of the Tatmadaw's crimes. Rather than empty calls for compensation or justice (which are meaningless until the SAC is dislodged from power) the world must act to stop the killing.

Other than a handful of incredibly poorly designed sanctions, the world has done virtually nothing. The West must provide material support to Myanmar's democratically elected government, the NUG, which has also promised citizenship for the Rohingya, and dismantle the pipeline of arms being supplied to the Tatmadaw by Russia, China, India, Singapore, and Thailand.

comments.name: Pat
comments.body:
Though the article states that atrocities were committed by the Buddhist majority (as well as other ethnic groups), the Buddhist majority has no right to claim they follow the Dhamma. 

No Buddhist who understands and follows the Four Noble Truths would kill or harm a living being on purpose. It is part of the forth Noble Truth in the Eightfold Noble Path, in the morality elements. I undertake to keep the training precept to abstain from killing or harming living beings on purpose.

This is just mundane human beings filled with greed, hatred, and delusion killing other human beings and they have no justification to claim they are Buddhist.

Many ALL beings be happy and safe!

comments.name: JC
comments.body:
I remember the before and after pictures how they just bulldozed.
Sad it takes so long to name it what it is and some still deny it justice by not giving it the name it deserves.

articles.title: Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya, Top Global Court Finds
articles.summary: In a decision with potentially broad implications, the International Court of Justice found a state culpable of genocide for the first time.

comments.name: Vince
comments.body: I was choosin' Texas once.  During a job interview, the interviewer asked me which state I would choose to eject from the union and why.  I did not hesitate in choosin' Texas.  I got the job the next day.  My sentiments remain unchanged, for both the state and the song.

comments.name: Denver
comments.body: I just listened to Vince Gill and Lainey Wilson’s tribute to Dolly Parton. What Lainey, and so many performers don’t understand, is that the way to sing a song like “I will always love you” is to sing it quietly. That allows the listener to reach deep down inside and find those moments of our own. Performers like Vince Gill (listen to him sing Go Rest High on That Mountain” and not be moved) understands. Too often singers resort to belting out a song at the same intensity and we get caught up in that rather than the lyrics. Chris Stapleton is one of the few current artists that I can say understands this also.

comments.name: Dwight
comments.body:
After an eternity of bropopcountry, it’s great to finally see the pendulum start swinging back the other way. 

Ella and Kacey and Miranda and Stapleton and Wilson are all authentic, supremely talented artists who carry the torch of authentic country music.

I sincerely hope Ella is correct in her assertion: “We’re just get started.” More of this, please.

For general information:  "salmon sperm DNA" has been available for purchase, in bulk, for laboratory investigations for more than 60 years; originally from Sigma Chemical Co of St.Louis.  It was used extensively as a "carrier DNA" in experiments requiring the precipitation of small amounts of recombinant DNA and for blocking Southern and northern blots so that radiolabeled DNA and RNA probes wouldn't stick to them randomly. comments.name: JBP
comments.body: I'm 95% fountain pen user the last 20 years. Every now and then acrylic and felt-tip markers. I couldn't go back to a regular pen at this point. There's nothing as pleasurable as writing with a properly tuned nib--I like my flow leaning wet and juicy! I love that there is a unique language to learn regarding the parts of the pen and other elements to its use. I've been to many a fountain pen show and have a few nibs with custom grinds by nib meisters that feel as if I'm writing on air they are so perfect in my hand. I love the variety of inks--I have probably 75 bottles of ink from ink scientists from around the globe ranging from Poland (which have a slight scent of vanilla to them) to Australia. But, yeah, looking at my fingers on my right hand while I write this comment, there are a couple of ink stains on my finger tips. I've grown to even like that. It's a sign that I am still a human, still writing with an implement that is both perfect and imperfect, kind of like humans.

comments.name: Craig Pinkus
comments.body:
I've written with fountain pens exclusively for the last 60 years or so. Why? First and foremost the feel. Heft. The fabric of the paper. The flow of the ink. The lifts and lowers that make the sensations of an "f" so different from an "o." 

Then aesthetics. The thicks and thins are just short of calligraphy. 

Not fast enough? Skill is required for speed, but with practise it's just as fast. Mr Dickens got a lot of words on paper. You say it takes too much maintenance. Yes, it takes time to refill, clean, and store if you have several. 

But what you don't mention whether or not the book does: the toxicity of ball point ink compared to fountain pen ink. The former must have non-pigment additives to flow--a little hole is not enough. And on landfill disposal, you'll find an unlimited supply of those throwaway pens. Try finding a Visconti, Cartier, Montblanc, and their kindred. 

The final difference between all ink handwriting devices and keyboards is the most important, hopefully recognized in the book: brain studies show they light up different areas. If you seek creativity and want to avoid the flat voice of AI, use handwriting.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body:
Our current fashion for doing everything we can on computers, laptops, or smartphones may be a passing trend; in fifty or a hundred years pen and paper may be in vogue again, at least for some applications (perhaps more sustainably, with more environmentally-friendly pens and paper; can we imagine biodegradable pens, and ink that breaks down safely in soil?)

My pen of choice is a Bic Round Stic.  Humbler even than the Cristal, but cheap, ubiquitous, comfortable in my hand, and durable.  I somehow avoided picking up the habit of chewing on writing implements, always keep the caps on one end or the other, and keep using them until the ink stops flowing.  Which, I like to think, means that I might only have to discard a few of them each year—if that.

My father had mugs full of fancier (but still ball-point) pens in four colors always standing by.  Lovely pens, with retractable points, fun to take apart and reassemble.  But alas all long dry.  Especially the glorious green ones!  Green ink must tend to be sticky or dry out fast.  Now I make do with boring, but reliable blue, except for special occasions, when I use a green gel pen.

Compared with the multitude of plastic straws discarded on a daily basis, the waste in plastic pens seems minor—especially if minimized through thrifty use.  Even with word processors, the humble pen still has its practical uses.  It's good to know that some folks still appreciate the instrument of the written word.

comments.name: Jim Brokaw
comments.body:
A solution is simple. Data centers should be required to generate all their power themselves, or buy it, using only renewable sources. This power sourcing must have no impact on local power rates or availability. Water for the data centers must be obtained without impacting local water supplies, and must be returned to it's origin (river, lake, or well) in as clean or better purity than it was draw at, and at the same temperature. And the boundaries of the data center property should be no noisier after the data center is in full operation than before it was constructed. That's what a truly "zero impact" data center would be like, never mind what industry and trade-group shills say.

Now, doing all this is going to require the data center companies to buy a lot of land, and invest a lot of money in renewable power generation on that land (solar, wind, and storage) or buy power from those sources where the installations are. And the water is going to need a purification and cooling plant. Maybe it would just be easier to build data centers somewhere away from towns and cities, and where land is cheap, solar power is plentiful, and water is readily available. Which would not be rural farm country in populous states, or in the middle of cities. With high-speed fiber backbones, there is not really a technological necessity for these data centers to be in cities and near population centers.

A.I. is going to bring on a future that is fraught with peril.  Assurances from CEOs of A.I. companies are totally worthless.  The best thing that the human race could do is totally eliminate A.I. just as the total elimination of nuclear weapons would be a great boon for humanity.

They use 2% of all electricity in the US--more than NYC and Los Angeles combined.  The general public pays for the generating costs of that electricity through their utility bills.  In a time when the Colorado River is at historic low water, data centers use huge amounts of it and there are reports that the water becomes polluted.  For what?  To line the pockets of the tech oligarchs with minimal benefit to the public and clear risk as the data centers hold our private data harvested by the tech companie. comments.name: Marco
comments.body: This is an interesting hybrid. Aside from other PBCs, there are other precedents for the trust, including the Dutch stichting (foundation) controlled company (with some associated corporate governance abuses) and the TIAA Board of Overseers. Paul Volcker was a member of that TIAA board for a time, now echoed by Ben Bernanke's role on the Anthropic trust. There has been tension at times between TIAA business incentives and its mission as originally defined by founder Andrew Carnegie, but much less intense than what Anthropic faces in that TIAA never had publicly traded stock. It does seem like the Anthropic 50.1% control for founders is a signal of control for the founders, who will have incentive to maximize share price. At least this is a group, rather than one individual.

I imagine corporate counsel would not want to see minutes published but what about an annual statement from the Trust summarizing key topics? Will its members be allowed to speak to investors and the press or will all communication be funnelled through IR? I think the Trust is an interesting and worthy effort but wonder how much influence it will have when push comes to shove.

comments.body:
"Russians will interject “Rock 'n' roll is dead, but I am not” into a conversation, for example, to mean that life endures amid the struggle." The line is actually "Rock and roll is dead, but I'm not - yet."

The stress in his name is on the last syllable: GrebenshiKOV.

comments.name: James I A
comments.body: What stayed with me most was how beautifully Apted captured the struggle of a young soul who feels this overwhelming need to do something meaningful through music, yet isn’t quite ready for the enormous changes that come with it. There is something so honest and deeply human about that contradiction. And I think the way the story was shaped in post-production is just remarkable. Watching it unfold, knowing everything that later happened between rusa and Ukraine, gives the film an entirely different emotional weight. It’s such a powerful reminder of how unpredictable life and history really are. We make plans, chase dreams, hesitate, hope… never knowing what tomorrow might bring. A beautiful and heartbreaking testament to a time none of us could have imagined would change so dramatically.

comments.name: Jane
comments.body:
It’s hard to describe what BG and Aquarium meant to us in the 80s in the USSR. Listening to their music on reel to reel copied from someone else. They opened our eyes to so many types of music, and philosophies. Seeing them live while visiting Moscow from Kyiv (back then it was a normal thing to do), was one of the most thrilling events in my life.
Telling the truth about the Soviet, and now Russian society,  has always been a big part of Grebenschikov’s work.
I loved the documentary, it was such a slice of life, and an interesting contrast on how different musicians work in different societies.  The oppression of Soviet Union forced Aquarium into the kitchen of a communal apartment to create their beautiful music with no time constraints, but no income.
Capitalism wanted to put him in box that would sell.
I still see BG whenever he comes to NYC
Thanks for profiling him and the movie

comments.name: TS
comments.body: Can’t wait to see the documentary! Very interesting piece

comments.name: Amanda
comments.body: Grebenshchikov heralded a spirit of freedom that helped pave the way for economic, political and cultural reform that centered in Leningrad in the late 1980s/early 1990s-- reform that ironically Putin got to enjoy when he returned there from Germany after the wall fell. Putin enjoyed the creativity and openness at that time that included the permission of small privately and cooperatively owned businesses for the first time in decades like farmers markets, small privately owned restaurants, stands outside of subways that sold flowers and snacks, flea markets etc.  allowed for the first time in decades. He thrived under the kindness and wisdom of his mentor and former law teacher mayor Sobchak. And as Putin benefitted and benefitted, he showed his gratitude by (probably) having Sobchak killed, becoming a tyrant and punishing/murdering all those who dare show any creative, living spirit. Putin is petty and jealous of truly talented, vibrant spirits . Tyrants -- Hitler and Trump included-- yearn to be admired but never will be truly loved because they aren't loving themselves. Thank you for your humanity and spirit, Mr. Grebenshchikov!

comments.name: Sasha
comments.body: The stress is on the last vowel:  greh-ben-schi-KOV).

comments.name: Sylvia
comments.body: Musicians Sasha and Yuri fled/left Russia in the 70s. Their agent was the son of Bill Graham, the San Francisco promoter. I interviewed them for my cable TV show at the time when no one knew any Russians, let alone Russian musicians, so they were looked upon with fascination. I think their embers of fame died out pretty quickly. Probably only known in the California music scene.

comments.name: Engaged Citizen
comments.body: I know I saw Aquarium in the late '80s in D.C. Unfortunately, I can't find anything online regarding a tour. They played to a small crowd that indeed hoped for more punk-sounding music, but in retrospect, they were the true rebels.

articles.title: A Russian Rock Musician With a ‘Need to Rebel’
articles.summary: In the 1980s, Boris Grebenshchikov led a revered Russian underground band. A rereleased documentary from that era is bringing new attention to his work.

comments.name: SMB
comments.body: If Google wants to go all in on AI, very simple solution: Drop Google. Duck Duck Go, Firefox, we have other - and far safer - choices than just jumping through tech's latest hoops.

comments.name: mbh
comments.body:
A note to Google and the other tech companies: in my world, the "best customer experience" does not contain chatbots of any kind. I used Google search extensively for professional reasons for nearly 25 years and strongly object to Gemini, and have now switched search engines though I still use Chrome.

Putting Gemini into Google search objectively makes it less useful.

comments.name: Jake Wagner
comments.body:
In the short run, Alphabet (Google) makes its money with ads.  But in the long run, Alphabet has a stake in numerous ventures that may eventually use AI.  Thus a short run fall in ad revenue may be offset by a long range increase in applications of AI which may be more important than advertising.

For example, there is the protein folding problem which was solved via a branch of Alphabet called DeepMind.  Eventually, this may grow into a technology that in conjunction with pharmaceutical companies uses AI to develop new drugs.

Another application is self-driving cars.  Yes, this is what Musk is trying to do.  But Alphabet is large enough to compete with Musk on self-driving cars.  And it contains Waymo which is a key player in developing self-driving cars.

It disturbs me that so many people see advertising as a "legitimate" use of AI.  That is really just using AI to manipulate the desires of individuals in the US.  And it seems inconsistent with Enlightenment Principles, which were based on the notion of people thinking for themselves, NOT responding to well-crafted advertisements.

In fact, I find the constant advertising of our society to be troubling.  It represents a trend in which the large corporations regard the "guidance of the little people" as a legitimate business model.

That makes democracy completely unfeasible.

Why don't people see that?

If you are happy to say goodbye to democracy, then yes support advertising to the hilt.  But I don't support that.

comments.name: P.G. Cavendish
comments.body:
For users of search, there are alternative such as Duck Duck Go. You don't have to use their AI function.
If you don't like Google, don't use it.

comments.name: Chris B
comments.body:
The model's the same as it ever was: build a good enough service to hold a monopoly and lock in users and advertisers, then enshittify it to maximize profit later, more ads, worse results, on to infinity.  
    They just haven't perfected the first stage of it yet.  As soon as they do, as soon as they're really confident that all search goes through the chatbot and will stay there, they've got their monopoly and users all locked in, then the AI will start to sound like a cheap salesman trying to sell you everything under the sun.  It's inevitable...

comments.name: Bart
comments.body: Google should start following up with users who searched certain categories and clicked through on AI answers. Companies could pay for the follow ups, if Google recommends a product or service in the follow up and users click through. There would be actual intent there, and companies would deal with fewer tire kickers and flakes.

Switched to Duck Duck Go and dont miss the google search at all.

You Tube, owned by google, is impossible to work with as a channel operator. I honestly do not think there are any people left at that company. Just robots.

I did not vote for this man, but I'll tell you what, he changed history and I'm very proud of him.  For the owners who keep saying they love their horses, Why don't they try pulling the carriages themselves? These horses are being forced to labor in the summer, in the winter to carry dead weight on their backs for decades, until they drop dead, the unions couldn't care less. I do love the quaintness of the carriages, but this is a long time coming. But we should also be more thoughtful about what replaces these carriages. comments.name: Barbara
comments.body:
Honestly, a good (ie a bit over) TWO YEARS NOTICE is a very good lead time to find a new job!
Can someone explain why TWO YEARS NOTICE is A PROBLEM? I'd say it's really quite a gift. Add to that the fact that this issue has been on the table for quite some time now. and that the writing has been on the wall for.that time. 
I am not talking about the sentimental aspect of the issue - ie, any of the drivers whose primary motivation for this job is their Love Of Horses, has TWO YEARS to find another job caring for or somehow involving horses.

comments.name: George S.
comments.body:
Sounds like a "takings".

I have mixed feelings about horse-drawn carriage in CP.  The quaintness is understandable but one is also concerned for the animals's welfare.

Oh, and as a cyclist who occasionally passes through the Park there is an additional negative aspect to consider.

But the reality remains that the City is prohibiting a long legitimate means of transportation.  One which it charged drivers for medallions to do business.

Vague assurances of some kind of "compensation" are insufficient.  

Follow the principles of condemnation law and appoint an independent arbiter to determine what fair compensation should be awarded to the carriage drivers.

comments.body: What is the pleasure in being the owner of a mega-million dollar piece of art, if you hide it away in a vault or hang it in your mansion for no one else being able to see it? I have no sympathy at all for auction houses losing money in this business. It's all obscene.

comments.name: Anne Kaier
comments.body:
Van Gogh died in poverty, having sold only one painting during his life. It’s heartbreaking to see these prices and think of that. If only the US would support young artists! I live in Philly where grads of our great art schools such as Pafa, struggle to get by. A country that loves actual art would support these painters. What governmental support we used to have has, of course, been decimated by the Trump administration.
These stories in the Times are always about money and art politics, never a word about the beauty of the art itself. Sad and infuriating.

Guyana’s President Mohammed Irfan Ali and before him her Vice-President Bharrat Jagdeo has been shouting from the rooftops that the world leaders especially the United States of America  need to get busy and stop kicking the can do the road before it gets too late for the world to do anything. comments.name: MLC
comments.body: Dimmers.   And more dimmers.  And some more.   I've got a mix of overhead lights (traditional chandelier-type), modern track elsewhere, and some recessed, along with the usual lamps, wall sconces, etc.   *Everything* is on a dimmer and adjustable.   Use dimmable bulbs, and the right dimmer switches, and you can have a bit of overhead when you want a little boost to the lamps, or crank it up when you need to do a deep cleaning on a gray and dark day.

comments.name: Marie
comments.body: My rental has those overhead round LED ceiling lights throughout and they drive me nuts. The ceiling is relatively low and I can't do anything without getting a huge shadow over my work or my book. They're awful.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
I have small pupils, which is why at age 68 I don't need reading glasses—also true of a first cousin, who's 79.
The flip side of that is that my night vision isn't good, and getting worse with age. That's true of most when they get older, and bright lighting from overhead or anywhere else has been shown to reduce the risk of falling.

comments.name: Elizabeth
comments.body:
3000K is still way too cold for me — and most people. Finding decent 2700K bulbs has gotten easier, but if you want 2400K, which give you that golden glow of old incandescents, it's tough at higher output levels.

But there are newer bulbs on the market now that let you set the Kelvin value with an app, from 2400 to 4000 or 5000. Much as I hate tech where you need to use an app, with these bulbs you set the K value and that's it (unless you want to change it later). So even if the app stops working or you delete it, the bulb works fine.

The bigger problem is built-in overhead lighting with integrated LEDs where you can NEVER change the bulb. So whatever the builder specified, you're stuck with unless you replace the entire fixture. 

This is even becoming the norm in simple flush-mount fixtures. It's a bad trend. These fixtures are supposed to last 20 years, but a lot of them are cheap junk that will burn out in less than 10.

comments.name: tunaboy
comments.body:
I remember reading about the model who, after years of working with photographers, knew a thing or two about light.
When at a party she would seek out a location with good lighting that enhanced the feature she was best known for and had spent years taking care of and refining; her “look”. No need for her to roam about, just hang out in the good light and let the party come to her on her terms.

There’s not always a dim bulb behind a beautiful face.

comments.body: The only reason I use my overhead lights in every room except the kitchen is for cleaning.

comments.body: This is very heavy on the excitement and rather light on how Anthropic is going to generate the sales and profits that will justify the IPO price, particularly  given the hundreds of billions of spending commitments that are coming up.

comments.name: Bill Cullen, Author
comments.body:
Interesting to me, at 1:09 PM, while the headlines are shouting, Anthropic Shares Soar in First Trades, my stock ticker now shows them down below where they opened at $95.42.

So they soared to a high of $115.00 and then crashed back down. If you bought in at that $115 your investment is down 20% in about an hour. But that can change and probably will. 

This isn't to say that this initial evaluation isn't newsworthy, it's incredible... but it feel like real headwinds for their segment at the moment. 

Will be interesting to watch this one, trading at $94.31 at the moment. Better adjust those front page arrows...

comments.name: RCarroll
comments.body:
The IPO is unrelated the extent of an AI bubble.

AI companies have borrowed huge sums of money.

There is considerable public resistance to data centers.

As someone retired from the high tech industry and having used software products for my entire adult life, it is not clear to me why I would purchase an AI product.

The recent GAO report about the chagpt-like products should alarm everyone.

AI and data centers are being forced on us without any regulation at the federal or state level.

comments.name: Blue Dot
comments.body:
This is the equivalent of building a nuclear reactor without any real planning or testing and hoping that it will all work out.

We all know that an Anthropic AI agent broke out of its "sandbox" and recruited other agents which worked together as a "collective" which eventually ended up hacking into an archive of other AI implementations in order to solve its "problem".

We also know that AI agents are very good at finding vulnerabilities in commonly used software. Recently, security exploits in software that almost all companies and government security agencies use.

This is technology that can do practically anything, is exponentially smarter than most human begins, and, as far as we know, has no moral compass or ethical foundations, and we're just going to let it out of the box and hope it doesn't do something very, very bad.

I wonder what AI would have to say about the intelligence, logic, or wisdom of doing such a thing? But, I suppose no one involved had the forethought to ask it.

The fact is, this technology could cripple the entire planet and bring not only the entire global financial market to its knees, but the human race itself before anyone knows what happened. But, all that is irrelevant isn't it, as long as there is trillions of dollars to be made. 

Pandora opened a box that unleashed plague after plague upon the world, but at least she did it out of curiosity. Alas, this box will be opened for something far more base and inane. Human greed.

comments.name: Observer
comments.body: Next: the great crash.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
These energy intensive AI data centers are driving up electric rates and complicating efforts to decarbonize energy production in order to avoid the worst impacts of the climate crisis.

And AI is coming for many peoples’ jobs.

All to build what many experts believe to be an existential threat. 

And for what? To make already wealthy people even more money.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
"Anthropic Has Gone Public. What Now?"

What now?  We wait for the next scandal from a board member that will shake the economy.  

We wait for Anthropic to sneeze and send shockwaves through the stock market. 

We wait for another infrastructure breakdown caused by AI.

We wait and watch another tech giant drive profits into its own pocket, destroying jobs, and hogging public resources for data centers. We watch as the average American sits  defenseless against this free-market capitalism.

We sit and watch as our supreme leader participates and profits from all of this in some way.

We watch the tech giants rule the world. And we watch AI rule our lives.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body:
I really hand it to Ms. Sarin and your production team for breaking down what would otherwise be a dry as paint subject like accounting, balance sheets and finance, and presenting it in an understandable and topical way.This beats reading S1 reports on my own hands down.
 
This format works much better than text only descriptions and highlights the key points for what is a really important topic. Bringing out the good, but especially the potential bad consequences from this particular IPO was illuminating. I don't know how a company that actually states under "Potential Risks" that their service may help bring down human civilization could be brought to market.But that's the time we live in.

Looking forward to more presentations like this from this team.

comments.name: Bethany
comments.body: This completes a major goal of the late Dr. Steve Ross, former board member at Chimp Haven and former Director of Lincoln Parks Zoo's Center for the Study and Conservation of Apes. He was my postdoc advisor and a wonderful person. Earlier in his career he worked to convince people who had chimps as 'pets' or used them in entertainment to relinquish the chimps to an accredited sanctuary or zoo. He worked with a coalition to lobby the Dept. of Fish and Wildlife to increase protections for captive chimps in the US. This was successful in 2015, effectively ending invasive biomedical research on chimps. It's great to see Steve's legacy unfolding. Also, Chimp Haven is a great facility - the staff is devoted to giving the residents the best retirement possible. They are highly deserving of donations - check out their website! I give and always dedicate my donations to Steve.

comments.name: Dianakmax
comments.body: As a lifelong Central Texan, driving past The Keeling Center has always been heartbreaking. While I am relieved that the chimps are finally heading to a sanctuary, we must not forget the thousands of other numerous types of primates still behind the fences that share 90% of our DNA. Rhesus macaques and baboons share 93 to 94% and all have emotional depth like humans. They will be assigned to other studies, breeding programs or euthanasia. I do want to acknowledge that from my limited understanding the Keeling Center is regarded across the board as one of the best as far as the care they provided.  Now...how would each of us feel if we had a child that was fighting for their life and this research depended upon it? What a hypocrite I would be.

comments.name: A Lady from Connecticut
comments.body: It breaks my heart that these wonderful sentient beings were used and then incarcerated for so long… now that we have the scientific means, let’s evolve completely away from using animals of any kind in our experiments.

comments.name: MEM

comments.name: dogperson

This goes for all their chimpanzees in my opinion. It shouldn’t fall on the public.

comments.name: KKW

comments.name: rickob

“Completing their transfers will fulfill N.I.H.’s commitment, announced in November 2015, to retire all N.I.H.-owned chimpanzees to sanctuary,” Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the agency’s director, said in a statement.

comments.name: SED
comments.body: I don’t see how anyone could argue that air power alone has won a war. It’s often been a sideshow to satisfy the bureaucrats in Washington until the dirty work on the ground can be accomplished.

comments.name: Devout Skeptic
comments.body:
I don't know about the books, but the review omits one important fact: that the American-Japanese conflict was the only one *ever* to be won by air power.

Also that the conditions for victory were created by Army and Marine infantry fighting their bloody way across the Pacific from island to island.

comments.name: Kevin Kelley
comments.body: See also Malcolm Gladwell's "The Bomber Mafia".

comments.name: Andrew Porter
comments.body:
But no mention of the 1942 book "Victory Through Air Power" and the 1943 Disney animated film of the same name? Both were extremely influential in deciding the course of WW2 and the future of US military aviation.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Through_Air_Power

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: If anyone is really interested in the subject, start with the Strategic Bombing Survey done in 1946. Nerd stuff, but is essential to understanding the topic. https://www.airuniversity.af.edu/Portals/10/AUPress/Books/B_0020_SPANGRUD_STRATEGIC_BOMBING_SURVEYS.pdf

comments.name: Vincent Amato
comments.body: Eventually, historians arrived at a consensus that Japan did not surrender because of the atomic bomb attacks on Hirroshima and Nagasaki.  The real cause of the surrender was that the Emperor feared that, with the entry of he USSR into the war, it would spell the end of the imperial system and the danger of Japan becoming a communist state.  Based on the behavior of the Japanese, its resorting to suicide pilots, women jumping to their deaths with their babies rather than facing surrender to the invaders and  a history of either never submitting or ultimately being saved at the eleventh hour by the intercession of their gods, there is a strong likelihood that the theory is a valid one. Many examples from the European theater of the war also support the ultimate impotence of bombing from the air.

comments.name: bf
comments.body:
Destruction of civil infrastructure in a first world country can hobble that society and make life there miserable. But it is far less effective at disrupting a more primitive society which is not as dependent on that infrastructure. 

Far more important than "winning the war" is the governance following the end of open hostilities, something which has been lost on those in power for the last several decades.

comments.name: Locho
comments.body:
"Those bombs, especially the atomic ones, hastened the American victory in the Pacific, making it the first time that air power actually delivered on its promise to end a war."

But to what extent was it air power that prompted the Japanese surrender versus sea blockade and widespread destruction of Japanese maritime assets? My understanding is that this distinction is the subject of a lively debate in the historiography, though I've read ostensibly serious history books that claim that the war was won through air power alone (see Immerwahr, How to Hide an Empire).

articles.title: How Much Can You Accomplish by Dropping Bombs?

comments.name: Gene Henry

comments.name: John R. Ross
comments.body:
Over my 37 years with New York City Transit, I had a front-row seat to the beating heart of this city. Day after day, I watched a remarkable cross-section of humanity step through those train doors—construction workers in dusty boots standing shoulder-to-shoulder with nurses coming off the night shift, doctors, accountants, lawyers, airline pilots, and flight attendants, alongside the tireless workers who keep our stadiums, restaurants, and hotels running. All of them bound for the same destination: keeping New York moving.

​Stories like this shine a much-needed light on our unsung heroes, yet they only scratch the surface. If you want to witness the true grit and soul of this region, step onto an early morning train out of the Flushing-Main Street terminal on the 7 line, or catch a pre-dawn Long Island Rail Road departure out of Ronkonkoma. Look around the car. That isn’t just a commute—that is the living, breathing backbone of New York, showing up before sunrise to build, heal, and serve. That is the real deal.

This is a great tribute, thanks again New York Times.

comments.name: gary gibbs
comments.body:
When I did my psychiatry residency at Albert Einstein in the Bronx I read an article When Your Brain is Prisoner of the State. It was about  a person who did not remember she had ECT until she read her medical records. She had lost all her memory of this time in her life. She became head of an organization agains ECT. The article also included an interview with the chief promoter of ECT , but overall it was critical as the title implied. I gave it to a secretary and asked her to distribute it . I wrote my name on the article as the provider. She said "You mean just give it to the residents  right? " I said "no, give it to everyone , the faculty and the residents." A couple days later she told me "You knocked their socks off, their stiff socks that is." 

At the end of the year I left the program and did a year of Osteopathic Manipulation residency at Kirksville College of Osteopathic Medicine, then decided to return to Einstein to finish my psychiatry residency but couldn't get in. I feel sure the article was the deciding factor .

So I finished my residency at St Luke's Roosevelt in Manhattan. I recognize for some people ECT has helped them, but has always been skeptical of what we were told was it only causing "soft" changes in memory. In my practice I had one patient who told me his brother had ECT and lost his memory of basic vocabulary. Another patient of mine did it against my advice, and was not happy with the result.

comments.name: Judy
comments.body: ECT modifies the neurons of the brain--by blasting them with electric shocks.   Memory loss suggests damage to those neurons.    Neurofeedback  on the other hand RETRAINS small groups of neurons in specific areas using only light or sound as rewards when a group of neurons fires at the right speed rather than too slowly (depression, for example) or too fast (ADD, for one).  Progress in treated areas is traced and charted by sensors on the scalp above them.  No shocks, no medications and no memory loss.   Patients are awake and not medicated.  Neurofeedback treatment takes time but is risk-free.  It changed my life, from constant anxiety and raging suicidal depressions to wonderful, productive  contentment.

No generator at the time, but I think a convenience store was open and we grabbed ice to put in the refrigerator. During Covid, a derecho came through and knocked out power. Fortunately we had a generator by then so our evening was fairly uninterrupted. Always have some cash on hand, even though I normally operate as cashless as possible. When we go places that call for at least 15 minutes of walking, she walks ahead of me because, as she responds when I complain, she likes to walk fast.  Although I can walk without assistance, I cannot keep up with her.  This has caused me to mentally cancel trips with her that call for that much walking, because she has already let me know that she does not want to slow her walk so that we are walking together. I wonder if other older parents with faster-walking adult children are experiencing similar issues.

comments.name: CarnW
comments.body:
I traveled quite a bit with my 80-something and then 90-something mother. A few tips: avoid travel in basic economy. The older traveler will be more comfortable if their long flights are at least premium economy. For my mother's 90th birthday, we flew her in business class (her first time ever in a premium class). My brother used his miles to fly in biz with her.

A full service hotel is a better bet than a hotel with minimal amenities. I made sure our hotels had a decent restaurant on site. We stayed at a hotel in Salzburg with a pleasant but not fancy restaurant serving dishes my mother liked. During our five days there, it rained every evening. Was so much nicer to just take the elevator down for dinner instead of going out. 

In addition, elderly travelers might appreciate amenities like a piano player in the lounge or lobby. After sightseeing with Mom, she enjoyed relaxing in the hotel lounge for an hour listening to the piano player and watching hotel guests come and go. 

Lastly, take them on a velo (bike) taxi tour. They can go to places off limits to cars and off the beaten path. The drivers are usually friendly and helpful. (plus most use e-bikes so you're not wearing them out)

comments.name: Ahem

Two questions I have learned to ask:

Are there stairs to get to the bathroom?

AirBnB owners are particularly bad at assessing whether their property is actually handicapped accessible. They forget that there are stairs from the driveway to the walkway. Or, my mother can get in the door, but can she get to the bathroom.

How high is the bed?

The nicer the hotel, the more likely the bed is going to be too high. My mother has lost several inches on her way to 95, and even handicapped accessible hotel rooms have beds that she cannot climb into. In fact, it’s this problem that has been the most significant factor in moving most family gatherings to her now, instead of taking her out for an adventure.

comments.name: DF

Lies are one of the tactics in the practice of gossip.  Since gossip has deep roots in human behavior we must make it clear that the stakes have again changed, imposing greater urgency & discipline on how everyone should deal with the sharp-tongued habit.

Now, artificial intelligence has added massive speed to the threat of nuclear extinction or breakdown in worldwide communication & control systems.  So we must sharpen our reaction regarding gossip.  Push back against everything more corrosive than idle gossip.  Ask tough questions after noting the weight of an accusation.  fe, "Such an accusation could lead to this person being arrested for a very serious crime.  If you have proof, why don't you inform law enforcement?"  Urgent.  Disciplined.

Good habits to control such gossip start with the individual.  These habits also help us ask the right questions when viewing our news sources.  If a solid majority of us push back against serious gossip including pseudo-news, we can pressure all (individuals & organizations) to grow up and act responsibly.

"[S]ometimes, a good-faith effort to be objective can in fact miss the mark . . .."  But is it a good-faith effort to be objective?

Whenever the Times reports on the number of Palestinians killed on a daily basis in Gaza, it makes a point of noting that the number does not distinguish between civilians and militants and that it comes from the "Gaza Ministry of Health, controlled by Hamas."  The use of the word controlled there carries a lot of freight.    

But whenever it quotes IDF spokespersons that an attack, which killed numerous civilians, targeted a militant, it does not likewise imply that the IDF's reporting is untrustworthy, only that it cannot be independently verified.  

It cannot be independently verified precisely because the IDF has prohibited unescorted reporters in Gaza, which in itself calls into question the veracity of the IDF's statement.  Yet the Times leaves it at a lack of independent verification.

Does that reflect a good-faith effort to be objective?

comments.body: When the judge said "if you stole money to buy a lottery ticket and won, you’re still a thief";  that concisely summarized the case. SBF pleadings; that no one lost money. (crypto paid off big time) is the red herring in all this. .If Julia Garner is listed in the credits..it's a watch: BigTime!
